The diagnostic pathway begins with elevated IGF-1 (age and sex-adjusted), followed by confirmatory oral glucose tolerance test showing failure of GH suppression below 0.4 mcg/L. MRI pituitary with gadolinium then localises the tumour. Treatment is transsphenoidal surgery for most patients, with medical therapy (somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant, cabergoline) reserved for unresectable or persistent disease. Complications include diabetes, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, and increased colorectal cancer risk.
key_points: IGF-1 is the initial screening test for acromegaly
75 g OGTT with GH levels is the confirmatory test - failure to suppress below 0.4 mcg/L is diagnostic
MRI pituitary follows biochemical confirmation
Colonoscopy screening is recommended due to increased polyp and cancer risk
explanation.pearls: The GH suppression threshold was lowered from 1.0 to 0.4 mcg/L (and some guidelines suggest <0.3 mcg/L) with the introduction of ultrasensitive GH assays, meaning historic cut-offs may underdiagnose acromegaly, particularly in patients with mild autonomous secretion.

options.rationale: Twenty-four-hour GH profiles are research tools and are not used in clinical practice for diagnosing acromegaly. The oral glucose tolerance test with GH suppression is the standard confirmatory test. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly Guidelines; eTG Endocrinology)

MRI pituitary is essential for tumour localisation but is performed after biochemical confirmation, not as the confirmatory test. A pituitary incidentaloma could coexist with normal GH dynamics, so biochemical confirmation must precede imaging to establish the diagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society; eTG)

While IGF-1 is the initial screening test and is elevated here, the diagnosis requires dynamic testing to confirm autonomous GH secretion. Repeating IGF-1 delays the diagnosis unnecessarily when the clinical picture and elevated IGF-1 already warrant confirmatory testing. (Source: Endocrine Society)

The insulin tolerance test assesses GH deficiency (stimulation) and cortisol reserve, not GH excess. In acromegaly, the confirmatory test is GH suppression with oral glucose. The insulin tolerance test is contraindicated in patients with epilepsy or ischaemic heart disease and is not the appropriate test here. (Source: Endocrine Society)

The 75 g oral glucose tolerance test with GH measurement is the gold standard confirmatory test for acromegaly. In normal individuals, GH suppresses to <0.4 mcg/L after oral glucose. Failure to suppress confirms autonomous GH secretion. This is performed after an elevated IGF-1 and before pituitary MRI. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly Guidelines; eTG Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is characterised by progressive deterioration in personality and social conduct with relative preservation of memory in the early stages. The Rascovsky criteria require at least three of: disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behaviours, hyperorality/dietary changes, and executive dysfunction. Onset is typically before age 65. MRI shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. Approximately 30-40% of cases have a genetic basis, with mutations in MAPT, GRN, or C9orf72 being most common. There are no disease-modifying treatments; management is supportive.
key_points: Behavioural change and personality deterioration precede memory loss in bvFTD
Rascovsky criteria require >=3 of 6 behavioural features
Frontal and anterior temporal atrophy on MRI is characteristic
30-40% of FTD cases have a genetic component
explanation.pearls: The C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion is the most common genetic cause of both FTD and motor neurone disease, and up to 15% of patients with bvFTD develop concurrent MND features, making neurological examination for upper and lower motor neurone signs essential at every review.

options.rationale: While disinhibition and impulsivity can mimic mania, the progressive insidious course over 18 months, primitive reflexes, frontal and temporal atrophy on MRI, and preserved memory distinguish this from bipolar disorder. Bipolar disorder presents with episodic mood disturbance, not progressive structural brain changes. (Source: NHMRC Dementia Guidelines; eTG Neurology)

Alzheimer disease typically presents with prominent episodic memory impairment early in the course. This patient has relatively preserved memory with prominent behavioural and personality changes, which is the hallmark of frontotemporal dementia. The pattern of frontal and anterior temporal atrophy on MRI also favours FTD over Alzheimer disease. (Source: NHMRC Dementia Guidelines)

DLB characteristically presents with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. Disinhibition and personality change are not core features. This patient lacks hallucinations and parkinsonism, and the MRI shows frontal atrophy rather than the more diffuse pattern of DLB. (Source: NHMRC Dementia Guidelines)

The progressive disinhibition, loss of empathy, compulsive eating behaviour, lack of insight, and relatively preserved memory are classic features of behavioural variant FTD. The MRI showing bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy is the characteristic imaging pattern. Primitive reflexes reflect frontal lobe dysfunction. Onset before 65 and positive family history are typical for FTD, which has a genetic component in 30-40% of cases. (Source: NHMRC Dementia Guidelines; eTG Neurology; Rascovsky criteria)

Vascular dementia presents with stepwise cognitive decline and focal neurological signs, with white matter changes on MRI. This patient has progressive behavioural change with frontal and temporal atrophy and no vascular changes on MRI, which is inconsistent with vascular dementia. (Source: NHMRC Dementia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is diagnosed clinically by the presence of concurrent upper and lower motor neurone signs in multiple body regions without sensory involvement. The revised El Escorial criteria require UMN and LMN degeneration spreading within a region and to other regions. EMG/nerve conduction studies confirm widespread denervation. Median survival from symptom onset is 2-5 years, with bulbar-onset carrying a worse prognosis. Riluzole extends survival by approximately 2-3 months. Multidisciplinary care involving neurology, respiratory, speech pathology, occupational therapy, and palliative care is essential.
key_points: Concurrent UMN and LMN signs in multiple regions without sensory involvement is pathognomonic
Normal cervical MRI is essential to exclude structural mimics
Bulbar involvement indicated by dysarthria, dysphagia, and tongue fasciculations
EMG showing widespread acute and chronic denervation supports the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Fasciculations in the tongue are highly specific for ALS when accompanied by tongue wasting, as benign fasciculation syndrome almost never involves the tongue, making this a critical discriminating sign during examination.

options.rationale: The combination of upper motor neurone signs (brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, spastic jaw jerk) and lower motor neurone signs (wasting, fasciculations) in multiple regions (limbs and bulbar) without sensory involvement is pathognomonic for ALS. The normal cervical MRI excludes structural causes. Bulbar involvement (dysarthria, tongue fasciculations) indicates bulbar-onset MND superimposed on limb-onset disease. (Source: eTG Neurology; MND Australia)

Cervical myelopathy can produce upper motor neurone signs in the lower limbs and lower motor neurone signs in the upper limbs, but the cervical MRI is normal, excluding this diagnosis. Cervical myelopathy does not explain the bulbar signs (dysarthria, tongue fasciculations and wasting) or the widespread fasciculations. (Source: eTG Neurology)

Multifocal motor neuropathy presents with asymmetric distal weakness and wasting without upper motor neurone signs. This patient has prominent UMN signs (brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, brisk jaw jerk) which are absent in MMN. MMN is also treatable with IVIG, making the distinction important. (Source: eTG Neurology)

Kennedy disease is an X-linked lower motor neurone disorder presenting with bulbar and limb weakness, fasciculations, and gynecomastia. Crucially, it does not produce upper motor neurone signs. This patient's brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, and brisk jaw jerk are UMN features that exclude Kennedy disease. (Source: eTG Neurology)

Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness without wasting or fasciculations, and reflexes are typically normal or reduced. This patient has prominent wasting, fasciculations, and upper motor neurone signs, none of which are features of myasthenia. MG also does not cause extensor plantars or brisk jaw jerk. (Source: eTG Neurology)

explanation.summary: DRESS syndrome is a severe drug hypersensitivity reaction characterised by a triad of rash, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement (most commonly hepatitis). It has a characteristic latency of 2-8 weeks from drug initiation, which distinguishes it from SJS/TEN (1-3 weeks) and AGEP (days). The most common causative drugs in Australia are allopurinol, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine), and sulfonamides. Management involves immediate drug cessation and systemic corticosteroids. HHV-6 reactivation is detected in many cases. DRESS carries a mortality of 5-10%, primarily from hepatic failure.
key_points: DRESS triad: rash + eosinophilia + organ involvement (usually hepatitis)
Latency 2-8 weeks distinguishes DRESS from SJS/TEN (1-3 weeks) and AGEP (days)
Allopurinol is among the most common causative agents in Australia
Facial oedema and lymphadenopathy are characteristic features
explanation.pearls: HLA-B*5801 testing before starting allopurinol is recommended in patients of South-East Asian, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, and African-American ancestry due to a strong association with allopurinol-induced DRESS and SJS/TEN, with the PBS now subsidising this pharmacogenomic test in at-risk populations.

options.rationale: SJS presents with mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital erosions), target lesions, and epidermal detachment, typically 1-3 weeks after drug exposure. This patient has no mucosal involvement, no skin blistering, has eosinophilia and hepatitis, and the 5-week latency is characteristic of DRESS rather than SJS. (Source: eTG Dermatology; ACD)

While viral exanthems can cause morbilliform rashes with fever, the marked eosinophilia (3.2 x10^9/L), significant hepatitis, facial oedema, and temporal relationship to allopurinol initiation make drug reaction far more likely. Viral exanthems do not typically cause this degree of eosinophilia or organ involvement. (Source: eTG Dermatology)

AGEP presents with acute onset non-follicular sterile pustules on an erythematous base, typically within 48 hours of drug exposure. This patient has a morbilliform rash without pustules, onset 5 weeks after drug initiation, and significant eosinophilia and organ involvement, which are features of DRESS rather than AGEP. (Source: eTG Dermatology)

DRESS (also called drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome) presents with morbilliform rash, facial oedema, fever, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, and internal organ involvement (hepatitis most common). The 2-8 week latency from drug initiation is characteristic. Allopurinol is one of the most common causative agents. The RegiSCAR criteria are used for diagnosis. (Source: eTG Dermatology; ACD; RegiSCAR Criteria)

Serum sickness-like reaction presents with fever, rash, arthralgia, and lymphadenopathy but typically lacks the marked eosinophilia and significant hepatitis seen here. The degree of organ involvement and the specific pattern of eosinophilia with facial oedema is more consistent with DRESS than serum sickness. (Source: eTG Dermatology)

explanation.summary: The 2017 Fleischner Society guidelines provide a risk-stratified approach to incidental pulmonary nodule management. For solid nodules 6-8 mm, management depends on patient risk: low-risk patients may have a single follow-up CT at 6-12 months, while high-risk patients require follow-up at 6-12 months then again at 18-24 months. Nodules >8 mm warrant either 3-month follow-up CT, PET-CT, or tissue sampling. Risk factors include smoking history, upper lobe location, spiculated margins, and emphysema. Volume doubling time assessment on serial CT is more sensitive than diameter change.
key_points: Fleischner guidelines stratify management by nodule size and patient risk
Solid 6-8 mm nodule in high-risk patient: CT at 6-12 months then 18-24 months
PET-CT has limited sensitivity below 8-10 mm due to partial volume effects
Stability over 2 years generally indicates benignity
explanation.pearls: Volume doubling time of 400 days or less on serial CT is highly suspicious for malignancy for solid nodules, and modern volumetric CT software can detect 25% volume increases that correspond to only 8% diameter increases, far exceeding the sensitivity of manual calliper measurements.

options.rationale: CT-guided biopsy of a 7 mm nodule carries significant complication risk (pneumothorax 15-25%) with a high rate of non-diagnostic sampling. For a nodule of this size without clearly malignant features, surveillance CT is the appropriate initial approach. Biopsy is reserved for growing nodules or those not amenable to surveillance. (Source: Fleischner Society; TSANZ)

Per Fleischner Society recommendations, a solid nodule measuring 6-8 mm in a high-risk patient (>30 pack-year smoking history) warrants follow-up CT at 6-12 months, then at 18-24 months if stable. Growth is assessed by volume or diameter change. Stability over 2 years of surveillance generally indicates benignity. (Source: Fleischner Society Guidelines 2017; TSANZ)

PET-CT has limited sensitivity for nodules smaller than 8-10 mm due to partial volume effects, resulting in a high false-negative rate. It is more useful for characterising nodules greater than 8-10 mm or for staging confirmed malignancy. Surveillance CT is preferred for 7 mm nodules. (Source: Fleischner Society Guidelines; TSANZ)

Fleischner Society guidelines recommend no follow-up for solid nodules <6 mm in low-risk patients, but this is a 7 mm nodule in a high-risk patient (30 pack-year smoking history). Follow-up CT at 6-12 months is recommended. Dismissing a 7 mm nodule in a smoker would risk missing an early lung cancer. (Source: Fleischner Society Guidelines)

Surgical resection without prior characterisation is inappropriate for a 7 mm nodule with smooth borders. The probability of malignancy for a 7 mm solid nodule is approximately 1-5%. Surveillance is the standard approach, with resection reserved for growing nodules or those with clearly malignant features on interval imaging. (Source: Fleischner Society Guidelines; TSANZ)

explanation.summary: PSA interpretation requires consideration of factors that alter PSA levels. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) reduce PSA by approximately 50% after 6-12 months of use, so the measured PSA should be doubled to estimate the true level. Other factors affecting PSA include recent DRE (minimal effect), UTI, prostatitis, ejaculation within 48 hours, and cycling. The free-to-total PSA ratio helps discriminate between benign and malignant causes, with ratios below 15% increasing the probability of cancer. Multiparametric MRI prostate is now recommended before biopsy.
key_points: Finasteride/dutasteride reduce PSA by approximately 50% - double the measured value
Free-to-total PSA ratio <15% increases probability of malignancy
Normal DRE does not exclude prostate cancer
Multiparametric MRI prostate is recommended before biopsy
explanation.pearls: The PSA halving effect of finasteride reaches steady state at approximately 6 months of therapy, and any subsequent PSA rise while on finasteride should be treated with heightened suspicion as it may indicate early prostate cancer growth overcoming the drug effect.

options.rationale: While repeat PSA may be appropriate to confirm elevation, the most important consideration is that finasteride halves PSA levels. A PSA of 6.8 on finasteride effectively represents a level of approximately 13.6 mcg/L off finasteride, which is markedly elevated and requires urgent further investigation rather than watchful waiting. (Source: USANZ/PCFA; AMH)

A normal DRE does not exclude prostate cancer. Approximately 25-30% of prostate cancers are not palpable on DRE, particularly in the anterior prostate or when the tumour is small. PSA elevation requires further investigation regardless of DRE findings. (Source: USANZ/PCFA Guidelines; RACGP)

5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) reduce PSA by approximately 50% after 6-12 months of use. The measured PSA of 6.8 mcg/L should be doubled to approximately 13.6 mcg/L to estimate the true level, which is significantly elevated and warrants urgent urological referral for multiparametric MRI and probable biopsy. (Source: USANZ/PCFA Guidelines; AMH; RACGP PSA Testing Guidelines)

A free-to-total PSA ratio below 15-25% actually increases the probability of prostate cancer. A ratio of 12% is concerning and supports further investigation. A higher free-to-total ratio (>25%) would be more reassuring and suggestive of benign prostatic hyperplasia. (Source: USANZ/PCFA Guidelines)

While age-adjusted PSA ranges exist, the critical issue is that finasteride halves the measured PSA. The true level is approximately 13.6 mcg/L, which exceeds age-adjusted thresholds by a significant margin. The low free-to-total ratio of 12% further increases concern for malignancy. (Source: USANZ/PCFA Guidelines; RACGP)

explanation.summary: Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis results from prolonged inhalation of organic antigens (avian proteins, moulds, chemicals). HRCT shows upper and mid-zone predominant ground-glass opacification, mosaic attenuation (reflecting small airways disease), and in chronic cases, fibrotic changes. IPF shows basal-predominant UIP pattern with honeycombing. Distinguishing chronic HP from IPF has critical management implications: HP may respond to antigen avoidance and immunosuppression, while IPF is treated with antifibrotics (pirfenidone or nintedanib). Multidisciplinary discussion involving radiology, pathology, and respiratory medicine is recommended.
key_points: Chronic HP: upper/mid-zone ground-glass, mosaic attenuation, exposure history
IPF: basal-predominant honeycombing, no identifiable cause
Serum precipitins support HP but can be positive without clinical disease
Multidisciplinary discussion is essential for ILD classification
explanation.pearls: Mosaic attenuation on HRCT is the radiological hallmark that distinguishes chronic HP from IPF, as it reflects small airways obstruction (air trapping) from bronchiolitis, which is a pathological feature of HP but not of UIP/IPF.

options.rationale: IPF characteristically shows a UIP pattern on HRCT with basal-predominant honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, and minimal ground-glass. This patient has upper and mid-zone predominant disease with mosaic attenuation and ground-glass, which is atypical for IPF. The history of pigeon exposure and positive avian precipitins point to chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis. (Source: TSANZ ILD Guidelines; ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT IPF Guidelines)

NSIP shows bilateral ground-glass with relative subpleural sparing, and is often associated with connective tissue disease. This patient has mosaic attenuation (air trapping) and positive avian precipitins with a clear exposure history, which specifically identifies chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis. (Source: TSANZ)

While sarcoidosis can cause upper and mid-zone disease, it typically shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and non-caseating granulomata. The mosaic attenuation pattern, pigeon exposure history, and positive avian precipitins are not features of sarcoidosis. Stage IV sarcoidosis presents with established fibrosis without ground-glass. (Source: TSANZ)

The combination of significant avian antigen exposure (pigeon fancier for 25 years), upper and mid-zone predominant ground-glass with mosaic attenuation on HRCT (reflecting small airways disease), fibrotic changes, restrictive spirometry, markedly reduced DLCO, and positive avian precipitins is diagnostic of chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Ongoing disease may occur despite cessation if fibrosis is established. (Source: TSANZ ILD Guidelines; ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT HP Guidelines)

Asbestosis is caused by asbestos fibre exposure, not farming. It produces basal-predominant fibrosis similar to IPF. Farming does not typically involve asbestos exposure. The upper and mid-zone distribution with mosaic attenuation and positive avian precipitins are inconsistent with asbestosis. (Source: TSANZ)

explanation.summary: Treatment of chronic hepatitis B is indicated when there is evidence of active viral replication (HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL), liver inflammation (persistently elevated ALT), and/or significant fibrosis. First-line nucleos(t)ide analogues in Australia are entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil, and tenofovir alafenamide, which have high genetic barriers to resistance. Lamivudine and adefovir are no longer recommended as first-line agents due to resistance. HBeAg-negative patients typically require indefinite therapy as relapse rates after cessation are high. Regular HCC surveillance with 6-monthly ultrasound and AFP is mandatory.
key_points: Treatment criteria: HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL + elevated ALT + fibrosis evidence
First-line agents: entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil, or tenofovir alafenamide
Lamivudine has unacceptable resistance rates and is not first-line
HBeAg-negative disease usually requires indefinite antiviral therapy
explanation.pearls: Entecavir resistance rates are <1.2% at 6 years in treatment-naive patients but rise to 51% at 5 years in lamivudine-experienced patients due to cross-resistance, making treatment history a critical factor in antiviral selection for chronic hepatitis B.

options.rationale: This patient meets treatment criteria: HBeAg-negative with persistently elevated ALT (>40 U/L on multiple occasions), HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, and evidence of significant fibrosis (F2 on FibroScan). Monitoring alone risks disease progression to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. (Source: GESA CHB Guidelines; ASHM B Positive)

While pegylated interferon is an option for chronic hepatitis B, it is generally preferred in HBeAg-positive patients where seroconversion is the goal, younger patients, and those with higher ALT. In HBeAg-negative disease with significant fibrosis, long-term nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy is preferred due to its better tolerability and the typically indefinite treatment requirement. (Source: GESA; ASHM B Positive)

Lamivudine has a high barrier to resistance development (up to 70% at 5 years) and is no longer recommended as first-line monotherapy for chronic hepatitis B. Entecavir and tenofovir have high genetic barriers to resistance and are the preferred first-line agents per Australian guidelines. (Source: GESA; ASHM B Positive; AMH)

FibroScan (transient elastography) has largely replaced liver biopsy for fibrosis staging in chronic hepatitis B. This patient already has a FibroScan showing F2 fibrosis, which, combined with persistently elevated ALT and HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, is sufficient to establish the treatment indication. Liver biopsy is not required before initiating therapy. (Source: GESA)

Entecavir is a first-line nucleoside analogue with a high genetic barrier to resistance (<1.2% at 6 years in treatment-naive patients). This patient meets treatment criteria: HBeAg-negative disease with persistently elevated ALT, HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, and F2 fibrosis on FibroScan. Tenofovir disoproxil or tenofovir alafenamide are equally appropriate alternatives. Treatment is typically indefinite in HBeAg-negative disease. (Source: GESA CHB Guidelines; ASHM B Positive; AMH)

explanation.summary: Severe alcohol-related hepatitis is defined by a Maddrey discriminant function >=32 or MELD score >=21, both indicating high 28-day mortality (30-50% without treatment). Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days is the standard of care, with the Lille score at day 7 assessing treatment response: a Lille score >0.45 indicates non-response and corticosteroids should be ceased. Contraindications to prednisolone include active GI bleeding, uncontrolled infection, and hepatorenal syndrome. Nutritional support and alcohol cessation counselling are essential adjuncts. Early liver transplant referral is considered for non-responders in select centres.
key_points: Maddrey DF >=32 or MELD >=21 defines severe alcoholic hepatitis requiring treatment
Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days is the standard treatment
Lille score at day 7 guides continuation - score >0.45 indicates non-response
Pentoxifylline no longer recommended following the STOPAH trial
explanation.pearls: The Maddrey discriminant function is calculated as 4.6 x (patient PT in seconds - control PT in seconds) + serum bilirubin in mg/dL, but in Australian practice using micromol/L and INR, the formula is modified: DF = 4.6 x (patient INR - 1.0) x 12 + bilirubin (micromol/L) / 17.1.

options.rationale: This patient has severe alcohol-related hepatitis based on the Maddrey discriminant function. DF = 4.6 x (patient INR - control INR) + bilirubin in micromol/L / 17.1. His DF exceeds 32, indicating severe disease with high short-term mortality. Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days is recommended, with Lille score assessment at day 7 to determine treatment response and guide continuation. (Source: GESA; eTG Gastro; EASL Guidelines)

N-acetylcysteine has shown benefit as adjunctive therapy with prednisolone in severe alcoholic hepatitis (improved 1-month survival in the AASLD trial) but is not recommended as sole therapy. It does not replace corticosteroids for severe disease. It is used as monotherapy only when corticosteroids are contraindicated. (Source: GESA; EASL)

Pentoxifylline was previously considered an alternative to prednisolone, particularly in the setting of contraindications. However, the STOPAH trial showed no survival benefit with pentoxifylline, and it is no longer recommended for severe alcoholic hepatitis by current guidelines. (Source: GESA; STOPAH Trial; EASL)

Ursodeoxycholic acid is used for primary biliary cholangitis and gallstone dissolution but has no proven benefit in alcoholic hepatitis. The jaundice here is from hepatocellular injury, not bile duct obstruction. Corticosteroids are the appropriate intervention for severe alcoholic hepatitis. (Source: GESA; eTG Gastro)

While nutritional support is essential (patients require 35-40 kcal/kg/day and 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day protein), supportive care alone is inadequate for severe alcoholic hepatitis with DF >=32, which carries a 28-day mortality of 30-50% without corticosteroid treatment. (Source: GESA; EASL)

explanation.summary: Pituitary apoplexy is a clinical syndrome resulting from haemorrhage or infarction of the pituitary gland, usually into a pre-existing adenoma. It presents with sudden headache, visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression), ophthalmoplegia (cranial nerves III, IV, VI), and hypopituitarism. The most critical immediate management is IV hydrocortisone, as acute ACTH deficiency causes adrenal crisis with cardiovascular collapse. Thyroxine replacement must be delayed until cortisol is replete. Neurosurgical decompression is indicated for progressive visual deterioration or reduced consciousness.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone is the most critical immediate intervention in pituitary apoplexy
Never start thyroxine before cortisol replacement in panhypopituitarism
Cortisol level <100 nmol/L in acute illness indicates severe deficiency
Neurosurgical decompression is indicated for progressive visual loss or reduced GCS
explanation.pearls: The rule of cortisol-before-thyroxine in panhypopituitarism exists because thyroxine increases hepatic cortisol metabolism via CYP3A4 induction, which in a cortisol-deficient patient can precipitate fatal adrenal crisis within days of starting levothyroxine.

options.rationale: While MRI provides superior imaging of pituitary apoplexy, waiting for MRI delays critical treatment. CT has already confirmed a haemorrhagic pituitary mass. The immediate priority is haemodynamic stabilisation with IV hydrocortisone, as cortisol deficiency causes life-threatening adrenal crisis. (Source: Pituitary Society Guidelines; eTG Endocrinology)

Pituitary apoplexy causes acute hypopituitarism. Adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency results in cortisol deficiency with haemodynamic collapse. The cortisol of 42 nmol/L confirms severe deficiency. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat must be given immediately, followed by 50-100 mg every 6-8 hours, before any further investigations or neurosurgical intervention. IV fluid resuscitation addresses the hypotension. (Source: Pituitary Society Guidelines; eTG Endocrinology; Endocrine Society)

Neurosurgical decompression may be indicated for progressive visual deterioration or reduced consciousness, but it is not the MOST CRITICAL immediate intervention. Without cortisol replacement, the patient is at risk of cardiovascular collapse during induction of anaesthesia. Hydrocortisone must be administered before any surgical planning. (Source: Pituitary Society Guidelines)

While the low free T4 and low-normal TSH indicate secondary hypothyroidism, thyroid replacement must NEVER be commenced before cortisol replacement in panhypopituitarism. Thyroxine increases cortisol metabolism and can precipitate adrenal crisis in a cortisol-deficient patient. Hydrocortisone must be given first. (Source: eTG Endocrinology; AMH)

While apixaban may have contributed to the haemorrhagic event, andexanet alfa is reserved for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding. The pituitary haemorrhage is typically self-contained and the immediate life threat is adrenal crisis from cortisol deficiency. Anticoagulant reversal is a secondary consideration after cortisol replacement and haemodynamic stabilisation. (Source: THANZ)

explanation.summary: Beta-thalassaemia trait is characterised by mild microcytic anaemia (Hb usually >90 g/L) with disproportionately low MCV, elevated red cell count, and normal iron studies. The Mentzer index (MCV divided by RCC) below 13 favours thalassaemia over iron deficiency. Confirmation is by haemoglobin electrophoresis showing elevated HbA2 (>3.5%). In pregnancy, partner testing is essential to assess the risk of beta-thalassaemia major in offspring. Pre-conception or early antenatal screening is recommended for high-risk ethnic groups.
key_points: Mentzer index (MCV/RCC) <13 favours thalassaemia; >13 favours iron deficiency
Normal iron studies exclude iron deficiency as the cause of microcytosis
Normal RDW with microcytosis suggests thalassaemia (IDA has elevated RDW)
Haemoglobin electrophoresis showing HbA2 >3.5% confirms beta-thalassaemia trait
explanation.pearls: In pregnancy, if both parents carry beta-thalassaemia trait, there is a 25% chance of beta-thalassaemia major in each offspring, making partner testing and genetic counselling before 16 weeks gestation essential per RANZCOG guidelines to allow time for prenatal diagnosis.

options.rationale: Iron studies are normal (ferritin 68, transferrin saturation 28%), which effectively excludes iron deficiency as the cause. In IDA, ferritin would be low (<20), iron low, and transferrin saturation low (<16%). The normal iron status points to a non-iron-related cause of microcytosis. (Source: eTG Haematology; THANZ)

Anaemia of chronic disease typically shows normal or elevated ferritin with low iron and low transferrin saturation. At 12 weeks gestation, physiological haemodilution has not yet significantly affected haemoglobin. ACD does not typically cause the degree of microcytosis seen here (MCV 64). (Source: eTG Haematology)

The combination of microcytosis (MCV 64) disproportionate to the degree of anaemia (Hb 108), elevated red cell count (5.8 - compensatory erythrocytosis), normal RDW (<14.5), normal iron studies, and Mediterranean ancestry is characteristic of beta-thalassaemia trait. The Mentzer index (MCV/RCC = 64/5.8 = 11) is below 13, supporting thalassaemia over iron deficiency. Haemoglobin electrophoresis will confirm elevated HbA2. (Source: eTG Haematology; THANZ; RANZCOG)

Sideroblastic anaemia is rare and typically presents with elevated iron stores (high ferritin, high transferrin saturation) and ring sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy. This patient has normal iron studies and a pattern more consistent with a haemoglobinopathy. Pyridoxine deficiency sufficient to cause sideroblastic anaemia is uncommon in a well-nourished patient. (Source: eTG Haematology)

While alpha-thalassaemia trait (two-gene deletion) can also cause mild microcytic anaemia with normal iron studies, it is more prevalent in South-East Asian and African populations. In a patient of Mediterranean ancestry, beta-thalassaemia trait is far more common. Alpha-thalassaemia is confirmed by genetic testing, not haemoglobin electrophoresis. (Source: THANZ)

explanation.summary: Post-cardiac arrest care follows a structured protocol: targeted temperature management, haemodynamic optimisation, coronary angiography if STEMI is suspected, seizure management, and delayed neuroprognostication. The TTM2 trial (2021) changed practice by showing no benefit of 33 degrees C hypothermia over normothermia with fever prevention. Current ANZCOR guidelines recommend targeted normothermia (<=37.5 degrees C) with active fever prevention for at least 72 hours. Neuroprognostication using multimodal assessment should not occur before 72 hours post-ROSC to avoid premature withdrawal of treatment.
key_points: TTM2 trial: no benefit of 33 degrees C vs normothermia with fever prevention
Current recommendation: targeted normothermia <=37.5 degrees C for >=72 hours
Active fever prevention is essential - fever >37.7 degrees C worsens outcomes
Neuroprognostication should not occur before 72 hours post-ROSC
explanation.pearls: Multimodal neuroprognostication at >=72 hours combines bilateral absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, absent N20 on somatosensory evoked potentials, highly malignant EEG, serum NSE >60 mcg/L at 48-72h, and diffuse cerebral oedema on CT/MRI, with at least two concordant poor prognostic indicators required before considering treatment withdrawal per ILCOR guidance.

options.rationale: The TTM2 trial (2021) demonstrated no benefit of 33 degrees C over targeted normothermia (<=37.5 degrees C) for neurological outcome after cardiac arrest. Current ANZCOR and ILCOR guidelines recommend preventing fever (>37.7 degrees C) rather than active cooling to 33 degrees C. Active hypothermia at 33 degrees C is no longer the standard recommendation. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.9; TTM2 Trial; ILCOR 2022)

The TTM1 trial showed equivalent outcomes at 33 degrees C vs 36 degrees C, but the subsequent TTM2 trial showed that even 33 degrees C provides no benefit over normothermia with fever prevention. Current best practice is targeted normothermia with active fever prevention rather than targeting a specific hypothermic temperature. (Source: ANZCOR; TTM2 Trial)

While active hypothermia is no longer routinely recommended, active fever prevention is essential. Post-cardiac arrest fever (>37.7 degrees C) is associated with worse neurological outcomes. Targeted normothermia at <=37.5 degrees C for at least 72 hours using active temperature control devices is the current standard. (Source: ANZCOR; ILCOR 2022)

Following the TTM2 trial, current ANZCOR and ILCOR guidelines recommend targeted normothermia (<=37.5 degrees C) with active fever prevention for at least 72 hours after ROSC. This involves continuous core temperature monitoring and active cooling measures if temperature exceeds 37.7 degrees C. Neuroprognostication should not occur before 72 hours post-ROSC. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.9; ILCOR 2022; ANZICS)

Rapid cooling to 32 degrees C is an aggressive hypothermia protocol that is not supported by current evidence. The TTM2 trial and HYPERION trial data do not support targeting temperatures below 33 degrees C. Rapid cooling can cause haemodynamic instability and arrhythmias. Targeted normothermia is the current recommendation. (Source: ANZCOR; TTM2 Trial)

explanation.summary: PsA is the unifying diagnosis: DIP joints, dactylitis, enthesitis, asymmetric pattern, seronegativity, and the pathognomonic radiographic combination of erosion with adjacent bone proliferation. RA is symmetric and erosive without proliferation; reactive arthritis follows GI/GU infection and has more knee/ankle large-joint disease without DIP predilection; gout produces tophaceous overhanging-edge erosions on a background of hyperuricaemia history.
key_points: PsA imaging hallmark: erosion + new bone formation (periostitis, pencil-in-cup later)
Dactylitis is highly specific for spondyloarthritis spectrum
DIP involvement strongly suggests PsA over RA
Skin psoriasis can postdate joint disease in 15% of PsA
explanation.context: Psoriatic arthritis sits in the seronegative spondyloarthritis family with shared HLA-B27 association, enthesitis-driven pathology and axial-plus-peripheral disease. The mechanism involves IL-23/IL-17 axis activation at entheses, driving local bone remodelling (both erosion and proliferation) - explaining why imaging shows both subtraction and addition of bone, unlike pure RA pannus-driven erosion. This mechanism is the rationale for IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) in PsA. In context, when an oligoarticular asymmetric arthritis presents with DIP involvement, dactylitis or enthesitis, PsA jumps to the top of the differential regardless of skin findings.

options.rationale: Dactylitis (whole digit swelling from combined synovitis, tenosynovitis and enthesitis), DIP-predominant disease, and the combination of erosion plus new bone formation are characteristic of psoriatic arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is symmetric, MCP/PIP/wrist predominant, with pure erosive change and no periostitis. Gout produces overhanging-edge tophaceous erosions, not periostitis (eTG; ARA classification).
Seronegativity is consistent with PsA but is also seen in 20-30% of RA and is present by definition in reactive arthritis and gout. It supports the diagnosis but does not discriminate (RACP).
Asymmetric oligoarthritis fits PsA, reactive arthritis and crystal disease equally. Without the imaging and dactylitis findings, this pattern alone does not separate them (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Inflammatory arthritis assessment

options.rationale: Urate may be normal during an acute gout flare (cytokine-driven shift). It weakly argues against gout but is not the strongest discriminator here; the imaging and dactylitis are (eTG).

Psoriasis history raises pre-test probability for PsA but only 30% of psoriasis patients develop arthritis, and PsA can precede skin disease. The discriminating features here are the imaging signature and dactylitis (CASPAR criteria).

explanation.summary: Pre-biologic screening in Australia: IGRA (preferred) or Mantoux, HBsAg + anti-HBc + anti-HBs, anti-HCV, HIV, varicella serology (if not immune, vaccinate before starting), and update non-live vaccines (pneumococcal, influenza, COVID-19, recombinant zoster). Live vaccines (MMR, yellow fever, varicella, live zoster) are contraindicated during bDMARD therapy.
key_points: IGRA preferred in BCG-vaccinated populations
Treat latent TB before bDMARD (isoniazid 9 months or rifampicin 4 months)
Hepatitis B reactivation occurs even in anti-HBc-positive HBsAg-negative patients (prophylactic entecavir)
Live vaccines contraindicated during bDMARD; complete before starting
explanation.context: TNF-alpha maintains granulomas that wall off Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacilli. Blocking TNF dissolves the granuloma, allowing bacillary escape and reactivation, typically with atypical (extrapulmonary, disseminated) presentations. This mechanism (mechanism inversion: a beneficial host response is the very thing the drug blocks) is why TB screening is non-negotiable. Hepatitis B reactivation follows a similar mechanism: immune suppression allows viral replication that the prior cellular response had contained, manifesting weeks to months later as a hepatitis flare.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association bDMARD prescribing checklist

options.rationale: Pre-biologic screen per the Australian Rheumatology Association and RACP requires testing for latent tuberculosis (interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) preferred over Mantoux in BCG-vaccinated or immunocompromised), hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), hepatitis C and HIV. Given Vietnam birth and prior Mantoux positivity she has high pre-test probability of latent TB; IGRA is more specific. Hepatitis B reactivation on TNFi is well-documented.
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association bDMARD prescribing checklist

options.rationale: TNF-alpha is essential for granuloma maintenance; blocking it reactivates latent TB within months. Symptom monitoring without screening missed cases historically and is below the standard of care (ARA).
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association bDMARD prescribing checklist

options.rationale: Mantoux false-positives are common after BCG (universal in Vietnam) and false-negatives occur on immunosuppression. IGRA is the preferred test in Australian guidelines for this population (ARA).
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association bDMARD prescribing checklist

options.rationale: JAK inhibitors require the same TB, hepatitis B/C and HIV screen as TNF inhibitors and additionally have herpes zoster, VTE and major cardiovascular event warnings. They do not avoid screening (ARA).
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association bDMARD prescribing checklist

options.rationale: Imaging detects active or healed TB but cannot exclude latent infection in the absence of IGRA or Mantoux. Latent TB management requires immunological evidence of infection plus exclusion of active disease (ARA).
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association bDMARD prescribing checklist

explanation.summary: GCA management: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg) orally immediately on clinical suspicion; if any visual symptoms add intravenous methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg daily for 3 days. Biopsy of the symptomatic temporal artery within 1-2 weeks, ideally with a 2 cm segment to minimise sampling error from skip lesions. Tocilizumab is steroid-sparing for relapsing or steroid-toxic disease.
key_points: Treat first, biopsy second - histology lasts 2 weeks
PMR overlap occurs in 40-50% of GCA
Visual loss is the feared, often irreversible, complication
Aspirin 100 mg daily reduces ischaemic events in GCA
explanation.context: GCA is a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis affecting branches of the external carotid (temporal, occipital, ophthalmic). The pathology is patchy (skip lesions), driven by IL-6 and interferon-gamma. PMR overlaps mechanistically via shared IL-6 elevation, hence dramatic CRP/ESR responses and the efficacy of tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor blockade). Jaw claudication has the highest positive likelihood ratio for biopsy-positive GCA among history features. Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy from posterior ciliary artery vasculitis is the emergency that drives the treat-first rule.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Giant cell arteritis

options.rationale: Histological features of giant cell arteritis (GCA) persist for at least 2 weeks on corticosteroid therapy, so steroids must not be delayed for biopsy. Australian and British Society for Rheumatology guidance: start high-dose corticosteroid immediately on clinical suspicion and arrange biopsy within 1-2 weeks. Sensitivity remains 70-80% in this window.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Giant cell arteritis
BSR GCA guideline (referenced in ARA materials)

options.rationale: Delaying steroids risks irreversible anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy and bilateral blindness. The Australian standard is treat first, biopsy second - histology survives the steroid effect long enough for diagnostic confirmation (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Giant cell arteritis

options.rationale: Halo-sign ultrasound is increasingly used as a fast-track tool (especially in the UK) but in Australia biopsy remains the reference standard outside specialist GCA fast-track clinics. Ultrasound complements rather than replaces biopsy (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Giant cell arteritis

options.rationale: Long-term high-dose corticosteroids carry substantial morbidity (osteoporosis, diabetes, infection); biopsy or imaging confirmation justifies prolonged treatment and is the standard (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Giant cell arteritis

options.rationale: Inflammatory changes persist at least 2 weeks; cancelling the biopsy abandons confirmation of a disease requiring 12-24 months of immunosuppression (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Giant cell arteritis

explanation.summary: ANCA-associated vasculitis induction: rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus tapering glucocorticoid (PEXIVAS reduced-dose regimen). Rituximab preferred when relapsing, fertility-preserving needs, prior cyclophosphamide exposure, or malignancy history. Maintenance after induction: rituximab 500 mg every 6 months (MAINRITSAN) for 18-24 months, or azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day as alternative.
key_points: Induction: rituximab OR cyclophosphamide + glucocorticoid
Plasma exchange only for severe DAH or anti-GBM overlap
Maintenance: rituximab pulses preferred over azathioprine for PR3-positive disease
PR3-positive disease relapses more often than MPO-positive
explanation.context: ANCA-associated vasculitis pathology: ANCA antibodies bind primed neutrophils (TNF-primed in infection or inflammation), triggering degranulation and release of neutrophil extracellular traps that damage small-vessel endothelium pauci-immunely (no significant immune complex deposition). Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells, removing the antibody-producing population. PR3-positive disease (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) is more relapsing than MPO-positive (microscopic polyangiitis), justifying scheduled rituximab maintenance. The bladder cancer history is the constraint-stack: it forces selection of rituximab over the otherwise-equivalent cyclophosphamide.

options.rationale: For PR3-positive granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) with organ-threatening disease, rituximab is non-inferior to cyclophosphamide for induction (RAVE, RITUXVAS) and is preferred when fertility preservation, prior cyclophosphamide exposure, or malignancy history is relevant. His bladder cancer history makes cyclophosphamide (bladder carcinogenicity, secondary malignancy risk) particularly inappropriate. Plasma exchange is reserved for severe alveolar haemorrhage or co-existing anti-GBM (PEXIVAS).

Effective induction but cyclophosphamide is contraindicated by prior bladder cancer (urothelial recurrence risk from acrolein metabolite). Rituximab is the standard alternative with equivalent efficacy (KDIGO).

PEXIVAS showed plasma exchange does not reduce death or end-stage kidney disease in ANCA vasculitis without severe alveolar haemorrhage. Reserved for diffuse alveolar haemorrhage or anti-GBM overlap (KDIGO).

Methotrexate is restricted to non-organ-threatening disease (NORAM trial). This patient has crescentic glomerulonephritis and lung cavitation - clear organ-threatening disease requiring rituximab or cyclophosphamide (KDIGO).
Steroid monotherapy is inadequate for organ-threatening ANCA vasculitis; relapse and progression to dialysis are near-universal without a second agent (KDIGO).

explanation.summary: APS anticoagulation: warfarin INR 2.0-3.0 for venous events, INR 3.0-4.0 (or warfarin + aspirin) for arterial events. DOACs are contraindicated in triple-positive APS, any prior arterial thrombosis, and discouraged in single/double-positive APS unless warfarin is unsuitable. Pregnancy: switch to LMWH plus low-dose aspirin.
key_points: Triple-positive = LA + aCL + anti-beta2-GP1 all positive
DOACs lose efficacy when the index event was arterial
Warfarin INR 2.0-3.0 for venous, 3.0-4.0 for arterial events
Lupus anticoagulant can prolong baseline INR - use chromogenic factor X if reliability uncertain
explanation.context: APS pathology: antiphospholipid antibodies bind beta2-glycoprotein-1 on endothelial cells, monocytes and platelets, activating complement, tissue factor expression and platelet aggregation. The procoagulant signal sits on the protein-protein interaction layer (slow, sustained, vitamin-K-dependent factor depletion countered by warfarin) rather than the active enzyme layer that DOACs target. This mechanistic mismatch explains why factor-Xa inhibitors are less effective: they block one downstream enzyme but leave intact the chronic endothelial activation that warfarin's broader factor-II/VII/IX/X depletion suppresses (mechanism inversion).

sources.label: THANZ position statement on DOACs in APS

options.rationale: The TRAPS trial was stopped early because rivaroxaban tripled arterial thromboembolic events versus warfarin in triple-positive APS patients. International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) and Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) advise against direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) in triple-positive APS and in any APS patient with prior arterial events. Warfarin remains the standard with target INR 2.0-3.0.
source_refs: THANZ position statement on DOACs in APS

options.rationale: Equivalence has not been demonstrated and TRAPS showed harm with rivaroxaban specifically in triple-positive APS. Class effect is presumed cautiously by guidelines until disproven (THANZ).
source_refs: THANZ position statement on DOACs in APS

options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is the specific agent that failed in TRAPS for triple-positive APS. INR monitoring inconvenience does not outweigh the arterial event excess (THANZ).
source_refs: THANZ position statement on DOACs in APS

options.rationale: Long-term LMWH is used in cancer-associated VTE but is not standard in APS. Warfarin remains first-line with reliable efficacy in this group (THANZ).
source_refs: THANZ position statement on DOACs in APS

options.rationale: Recurrent unprovoked VTE plus persistent triple-positive APS mandates indefinite anticoagulation; recurrence rate off therapy approaches 30% per year (THANZ).
source_refs: THANZ position statement on DOACs in APS

explanation.summary: Valvular AF (moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or any mechanical heart valve) requires warfarin, not DOACs. In non-valvular AF, DOACs are preferred over warfarin, with apixaban being the most renal-tolerant (used down to CrCl 25 mL/min, with caution below). The CHA2DS2-VA score (replacing CHA2DS2-VASc in Australia since 2024, dropping sex) guides anticoagulation initiation.
key_points: Valvular AF: warfarin only
Apixaban most renal-tolerant DOAC (>= 25 mL/min)
Dabigatran is 80% renal cleared - contraindicated CrCl <30
Aspirin is not an acceptable substitute
explanation.context: Mitral stenosis creates a low-flow, high-shear left atrial environment that activates platelet and contact-pathway thrombosis differently from the stasis-driven AF in structurally normal hearts. DOAC trials excluded patients with significant mitral stenosis, so efficacy is unknown and presumed inadequate. RE-ALIGN extrapolation (mechanical valves) showed harm. CHA2DS2-VA: C congestive heart failure, H hypertension, A age >=75 (2 points), D diabetes, S2 stroke/TIA (2 points), V vascular disease, A age 65-74. This patient has age, hypertension and vascular features driving the score.

options.rationale: Moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis defines valvular atrial fibrillation, where direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated (no trial evidence; the RE-ALIGN trial of dabigatran in mechanical valves showed increased thrombosis). Warfarin remains the standard. Severe renal impairment is an independent additional argument against DOACs but the valve lesion alone settles the choice.
DOACs are contraindicated in rheumatic mitral stenosis regardless of renal function. The renal dose-reduction question does not arise (NHFA/CSANZ).
Rivaroxaban is contraindicated in valvular AF and is also contraindicated when creatinine clearance <15 mL/min; this patient's valve lesion alone excludes it (NHFA/CSANZ; PI).
Aspirin is inferior to warfarin for stroke prevention in AF and is no longer recommended as an alternative; it offers minor benefit at substantial bleeding risk (NHFA/CSANZ).
Dabigatran is 80% renally cleared and is contraindicated at creatinine clearance <30 mL/min, and is contraindicated in mechanical and rheumatic valve disease (NHFA/CSANZ).

explanation.summary: Unprovoked proximal VTE: minimum 3 months treatment, then decide on extended therapy. Extended therapy is favoured in men, persisting risk factors, recurrent VTE or strong thrombophilia, unless bleeding risk is high. Low-dose DOAC (apixaban 2.5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) is the preferred extended regimen. Reassess annually.
key_points: 3-month minimum for proximal DVT
Extended low-dose DOAC for unprovoked DVT in men
HERDOO2 score can identify low-risk women safe to stop
Annual review of bleeding risk and preference
explanation.context: Recurrence risk after unprovoked VTE is sex-divergent: men 10% in year 1, women 5%, both rising cumulatively. The HERDOO2 score (Hyperpigmentation, Edema, Redness; D-dimer >250; Obesity BMI >30; Older age >65) identifies women safe to stop after 3-6 months (score 0-1) but is not validated in men, so men with unprovoked VTE default to extended therapy. AMPLIFY-EXT pivotal data: apixaban 2.5 mg BD vs placebo reduced recurrence from 8.8% to 1.7% with major bleeding 0.2% vs 0.5% - the rare situation where extended therapy improves both outcomes.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Extended VTE therapy
ISTH guidance on extended VTE anticoagulation

options.rationale: AMPLIFY-EXT showed apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily after the initial 6-month treatment phase reduced recurrent VTE by over 80% with bleeding rates similar to placebo. ISTH guidance and Therapeutic Guidelines endorse extended low-dose DOAC therapy for unprovoked proximal DVT in men (higher recurrence than women) and in patients with persisting risk factors (obesity here), absent high bleeding risk. Annual reassessment of bleeding and patient preference is required.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Extended VTE therapy
ISTH guidance on extended VTE anticoagulation

options.rationale: Three months is the minimum for proximal DVT but male sex and unprovoked nature give an annual recurrence of 7-10%, justifying extended therapy when bleeding risk is acceptable (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Extended VTE therapy

options.rationale: AMPLIFY-EXT showed 2.5 mg twice daily is equally effective at preventing recurrence as 5 mg twice daily in the extended phase with lower bleeding. Full dose is not required after the initial treatment period (ISTH).
source_refs: ISTH guidance on extended VTE anticoagulation

options.rationale: Aspirin (ASPIRE, WARFASA) reduces recurrence by only 30-40% versus 80%+ with low-dose DOAC and is reserved for patients who decline or cannot tolerate anticoagulation (ISTH).
source_refs: ISTH guidance on extended VTE anticoagulation

options.rationale: Low-intensity warfarin (PREVENT) is inferior to standard intensity and is not an Australian standard for extended VTE prevention. Apixaban 2.5 mg BD is the preferred regimen (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Extended VTE therapy

explanation.summary: Adult thrombotic microangiopathy differential: TTP (ADAMTS13 activity <10%, neurological prominent, AKI mild-moderate), aHUS (complement dysregulation, AKI prominent, neurology variable), Shiga toxin HUS (preceding bloody diarrhoea, children > adults), DIC (deranged coagulation, low fibrinogen). TTP demands urgent plasma exchange. ITP differs entirely: isolated platelet drop without MAHA.
key_points: TTP pentad: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + neuro + AKI + fever (full pentad uncommon)
ADAMTS13 <10% confirms TTP but treat empirically while awaiting
Avoid platelet transfusion in TTP unless life-threatening bleed
Caplacizumab (anti-vWF nanobody) reduces refractoriness in many centres
explanation.context: TTP mechanism: ADAMTS13 normally cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor (vWF) multimers released from endothelium. Acquired deficiency (autoantibody) leaves ultra-large multimers intact - they bind platelets and form microthrombi in capillaries and arterioles, especially in brain, heart, kidneys, mesentery. The microthrombi shear passing red cells (schistocytes, intravascular haemolysis - undetectable haptoglobin, high LDH) and consume platelets (thrombocytopenia). The mechanism inversion is therapeutic: replace ADAMTS13 (plasma) and remove the inhibitor antibody (exchange), then suppress production (steroid, rituximab). Caplacizumab blocks the vWF-platelet interaction directly, buying time.

options.rationale: Pentad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA, schistocytes + low haptoglobin + raised LDH + raised bilirubin), thrombocytopenia, neurological changes, fever and acute kidney injury (AKI) with normal coagulation defines thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) until ADAMTS13 returns. Untreated mortality exceeds 90%; treated 10-20%. Plasma exchange replaces ADAMTS13 and removes the inhibitor antibody. Steroids suppress antibody production. Caplacizumab is added in many Australian centres while awaiting ADAMTS13 confirmation.
source_refs: British Society for Haematology TTP guideline (HSANZ aligned)

options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in TTP fuels thrombotic microangiopathy and worsens neurological and cardiac events. Reserved for life-threatening bleeding only. The diagnosis here is TTP not ITP (HSANZ).

Eculizumab targets complement-mediated atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS). In adults with prominent neurology and only modest AKI, TTP is more likely; eculizumab is appropriate when aHUS is the leading diagnosis (after ADAMTS13 returns adequate) (HSANZ).

IVIg + steroid is first-line for adult immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), which presents with isolated thrombocytopenia without MAHA, AKI or neurology. This patient has the full thrombotic microangiopathy syndrome (HSANZ).
Fever in TTP is a syndrome feature, not infection-driven. Antibiotic-first delays plasma exchange and increases mortality. Cultures may be sent in parallel but exchange must not wait (HSANZ).

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia differential: iron deficiency (commonest), thalassaemia (microcytosis disproportionate to anaemia, normal iron), anaemia of chronic disease (usually normocytic, sometimes mildly microcytic), sideroblastic anaemia (rare). Iron studies are the first-line discriminator. In iron deficiency, treat the cause (menstrual, dietary, GI loss) and replace iron orally or intravenously.
key_points: Ferritin <30 microg/L = iron deficiency in non-inflamed states
Ferritin <100 microg/L with TSAT <20% suggests iron deficiency in inflammation/CKD
Investigate cause: GI loss in men and postmenopausal women
Oral iron alternate-day dosing improves absorption vs daily
explanation.context: Iron metabolism: hepcidin is the master regulator, released by the liver in response to iron stores and inflammation. High hepcidin internalises and degrades ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, blocking iron export to plasma. In inflammation, hepcidin is elevated even when stores are low, masking iron deficiency on ferritin alone - hence the higher ferritin threshold (100 microg/L with TSAT <20%) in chronic disease. Alternate-day oral iron dosing exploits hepcidin's circadian rise after a dose: a dose every second day catches hepcidin at its trough, doubling fractional absorption versus daily dosing.

options.rationale: Iron deficiency anaemia from menstrual losses and reduced dietary intake. Ferritin (iron storage) falls first, transferrin (iron-carrying capacity) rises as the liver upregulates synthesis to scavenge iron, and transferrin saturation falls. Ferritin under 30 micrograms/L confirms iron deficiency in non-inflamed states (eTG; RCPA).

This is anaemia of chronic disease: inflammation upregulates hepcidin, sequestering iron in macrophages (high ferritin), reducing transferrin synthesis and saturation. MCV is usually normal or only mildly low (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology - Anaemia of chronic disease

options.rationale: Inconsistent with microcytic anaemia. Suggests thalassaemia trait (microcytosis with normal iron studies) requires haemoglobin electrophoresis (eTG).
This is iron overload (haemochromatosis, transfusion overload) - the opposite metabolic picture and not associated with anaemia in this pattern (RCPA).
Internally inconsistent: low ferritin with high saturation suggests acute iron supplementation effect or sample after iron dose. Not a recognised iron deficiency pattern (RCPA).

explanation.summary: Macrocytic anaemia workup: distinguish megaloblastic (B12/folate deficiency, drugs disrupting DNA synthesis e.g. methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide) from non-megaloblastic (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, MDS, reticulocytosis). Film features (hypersegmented neutrophils, oval macrocytes) point to megaloblastic. Measure B12 and folate before replacement; replace B12 first (or together) if both low.
key_points: Hypersegmented neutrophils + oval macrocytes = megaloblastic
Metformin and PPIs both impair B12 absorption
Replace B12 before/with folate to avoid SCD precipitation
Neurological signs mandate parenteral B12 loading
explanation.context: B12 (cobalamin) is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase. Deficiency disrupts DNA synthesis (megaloblastic anaemia) and myelin maintenance (subacute combined degeneration of dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts - the unsteady gait and paraesthesia here). Side-effect-to-class reasoning: chronic acid suppression (PPIs, atrophic gastritis) reduces protein-bound B12 liberation; metformin disrupts ileal absorption. Both are common, both are reversible-cause checks before invasive workup. Folate replacement alone bypasses the haematological deficit but leaves neurological B12 deficiency to progress unchecked - hence the rule to replace B12 first.

options.rationale: Macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils and pancytopenic trend with neurological features suggest vitamin B12 deficiency. Metformin (impairs B12 absorption via altered ileal calcium-dependent uptake) and long-term proton pump inhibitor (reduced gastric acid impairs cobalamin release from food protein) are both contributors. Folate should be measured simultaneously - giving folate without B12 in combined deficiency precipitates subacute combined degeneration.

Useful if haemolysis is the leading diagnosis, but the film features (oval macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils) and neurological signs point to megaloblastic process, not autoimmune haemolysis (RCPA).
MDS is a differential for macrocytic anaemia in older adults but reversible causes (B12, folate, thyroid, alcohol, drugs) are excluded first. Bone marrow is later in the workup (eTG).
Hypothyroidism and alcohol excess cause non-megaloblastic macrocytosis (round macrocytes, no hypersegmentation). The film here is classically megaloblastic - go to B12/folate first (RCPA).
Coeliac disease can cause B12/folate malabsorption but is investigated after deficiencies are confirmed; serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA) precedes biopsy (eTG).

explanation.summary: CKD anaemia workup: confirm anaemia, exclude non-renal causes (iron, B12, folate, occult blood loss, haemolysis, MDS). Optimise iron first (target ferritin >100 microg/L and TSAT >20%; if dialysis, ferritin >200 and TSAT >20%). Start ESA when Hb <100 g/L and symptomatic, target 100-115 g/L. Newer agents: HIF-PHI (roxadustat) increasingly used.
key_points: Iron-replete first (ferritin >100, TSAT >20%)
Hb target 100-115 g/L - higher targets harm
Transfusion sparingly to preserve transplant eligibility
Investigate non-renal causes before attributing to CKD
explanation.context: CKD anaemia mechanism: reduced erythropoietin (EPO) production by peritubular fibroblasts as renal mass declines; uraemic inhibitors of erythropoiesis; absolute iron deficiency from chronic blood loss (dialysis, GI) and functional iron deficiency from inflammation-driven hepcidin upregulation sequestering iron. ESAs replace EPO but cannot drive erythropoiesis without iron substrate - hence iron optimisation must precede ESA initiation. The AU cut-off discrimination is the haemoglobin target band: 100-115 g/L balances symptom improvement against the cardiovascular harms shown when targeting normal-range haemoglobin in CKD.

options.rationale: Iron stores are adequate (ferritin >100 microg/L, TSAT >20%), reversible causes excluded, haemoglobin <100 g/L and symptomatic - erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) is indicated per KDIGO and KHA-CARI. Target haemoglobin 100-115 g/L; aiming above 130 g/L (TREAT, CHOIR) increases stroke and cardiovascular events.
TREAT and CHOIR showed that haemoglobin targets above 130 g/L increase stroke and cardiovascular mortality. Australian and KDIGO targets remain 100-115 g/L (KDIGO).

Iron stores are already adequate (ferritin 180, TSAT 28%); further iron does not improve haemoglobin and risks oxidative stress and infection. IV iron is given when ferritin <100 microg/L or TSAT <20% in CKD (KDIGO).
Transfusion in CKD anaemia is reserved for symptomatic acute drops, surgery, or failed ESA. It risks HLA sensitisation that complicates future transplantation (ANZSBT).
He is symptomatic with haemoglobin 92, iron-replete and B12/folate-replete; expectant management forfeits proven benefit (KHA-CARI).

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome triggers a vicious cycle: pain causes splinting and hypoventilation, hypoxia drives sickling, sickling causes pulmonary microvascular occlusion and infarction, releasing fat emboli from infarcted marrow. Multimodal bundle: oxygen, antibiotics (cefotaxime + macrolide or doxycycline), incentive spirometry, judicious analgesia, exchange transfusion for severe disease, and bronchodilators if reversible airway component.
key_points: Acute chest = new infiltrate + (fever OR resp symptom) in SCD
Atypical cover essential (mycoplasma common trigger)
Exchange transfusion if severe: SpO2 <90%, multilobar, falling Hb
Incentive spirometry prevents progression in pain crises
explanation.context: Acute chest syndrome mechanism: any pulmonary insult (infection, atelectasis from chest-wall splinting in pain crisis, fat embolism from infarcted bone marrow) reduces alveolar oxygen tension. Hypoxia in capillaries promotes HbS polymerisation, deforming red cells into sickles that occlude vessels and cause infarction - which further reduces oxygen tension. Exchange transfusion breaks the cycle by reducing the proportion of HbS in circulation rapidly (target <30%) without the volume load that simple transfusion would add to already-stressed pulmonary vasculature (mechanism inversion: the disease cell IS the problem; remove it rather than dilute it).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology - Sickle cell crises

options.rationale: Acute chest syndrome: new pulmonary infiltrate plus fever plus respiratory symptoms in sickle cell disease. Mortality 3-9%. Management is multimodal: oxygen, broad-spectrum antibiotics (cover atypicals - mycoplasma and chlamydia are common precipitants), incentive spirometry (prevents atelectasis from splinting pain), and exchange transfusion (preferred over simple transfusion when severe: SpO2 <90%, multilobar, falling Hb). Continue analgesia but titrate to avoid further hypoventilation.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology - Sickle cell crises

options.rationale: Acute chest is a respiratory emergency; opioid escalation alone risks further hypoventilation and progression. Definitive management combines oxygen, antibiotics, transfusion and chest physiotherapy (HSANZ).

Simple transfusion is acceptable in mild acute chest but exchange transfusion is preferred when severe (SpO2 <90%, multilobar infiltrates, falling Hb) - it reduces HbS percentage without volume overload (HSANZ).
Acute chest syndrome is not pulmonary oedema; diuresis worsens hypovolaemic sickling. NIV may be considered for severe respiratory failure but is not the primary intervention (HSANZ).
Antibiotics are necessary but insufficient. Atypical cover is required, plus oxygen, transfusion (exchange when severe) and chest physiotherapy - the bundle reduces mortality (HSANZ).

explanation.summary: Hot joint workup: aspirate before treatment. Send synovial fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal examination under polarised light. Even when crystals are present, infection can coexist - if any suspicion of sepsis, give empirical antibiotics after culture. Acute gout treatment: NSAID, colchicine or prednisolone; do not start or stop urate-lowering therapy during a flare.
key_points: Monosodium urate: needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent
Calcium pyrophosphate: rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent
Synovial WCC >50 x 10^9/L raises sepsis concern even with crystals
Treat presumed septic arthritis empirically pending culture
explanation.context: Gout pathology: monosodium urate crystallises in synovial fluid when urate concentration exceeds solubility (around 0.36 mmol/L at 37 degrees). Crystals are phagocytosed by neutrophils, activating NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta release, driving acute inflammation. The crystal shape (long needles) lyses lysosomes inside phagocytes, amplifying the response. Polarised light microscopy uses the crystal's anisotropy: negative birefringence means the crystal appears yellow when parallel to the polariser axis. Septic arthritis from S. aureus or streptococci dominates in adults; gonococcal arthritis (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) is a young-adult differential with tenosynovitis and dermatitis.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Gout vs septic arthritis

options.rationale: Monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent under polarised light. Sterile Gram stain (with culture pending) and elevated synovial white cell count up to 50 x 10^9/L are consistent with crystal arthritis. Septic arthritis typically shows neutrophils with positive Gram stain (in 50-70%) and synovial WCC frequently >50 x 10^9/L (eTG; ARA).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Gout vs septic arthritis

options.rationale: Calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout) crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent. Possible cause of an acute hot joint but the urate level and clinical pattern favour gout here (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Gout vs septic arthritis

options.rationale: Synovial WCC over 50-100 x 10^9/L without crystals strongly suggests septic arthritis until proven otherwise. This finding argues against gout (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Gout vs septic arthritis

options.rationale: Suggests Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis - the diagnosis to exclude before treating as gout. This finding mandates surgical washout and antibiotics (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Gout vs septic arthritis

options.rationale: Haemarthrosis points to trauma, coagulopathy or pigmented villonodular synovitis - not gout or sepsis (ARA).

explanation.summary: Reactive arthritis: post-infectious inflammatory arthritis 1-4 weeks after enteric (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or urogenital (Chlamydia trachomatis) infection. Asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis, enthesitis, conjunctivitis, sterile urethritis, sometimes circinate balanitis or keratoderma blennorrhagicum. HLA-B27 in 60-80%. Treatment: NSAIDs first, intra-articular steroids for persistent monoarthritis, DMARDs if chronic.
key_points: Triad: arthritis + conjunctivitis + urethritis (Reiter's)
1-4 week latency from index infection
NSAIDs first-line, antibiotics do not change course
HLA-B27 association; consider testing if chronic
explanation.context: Reactive arthritis pathogenesis involves immune cross-reactivity between bacterial antigens (transiently presented during enteric or urogenital infection) and self-antigens at entheses, plus HLA-B27 mediated misfolding/unfolded protein response in synoviocytes. The latency from infection to arthritis (1-4 weeks) reflects the time to develop the cross-reactive T-cell response. Most cases resolve within 3-6 months but 15-20% become chronic and indistinguishable from other peripheral spondyloarthritis. The mechanism inversion in management: antibiotics cure the trigger infection but cannot recall the cross-reactive immune response - hence NSAIDs/anti-inflammatory therapy, not antimicrobials, are the standard.

options.rationale: Reactive arthritis (the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis after enteric or genitourinary infection) is largely self-limiting within 3-6 months. First-line management is NSAIDs at full anti-inflammatory dose with PPI cover, plus physiotherapy. Antibiotics for the index Campylobacter infection are usually not indicated weeks later. Intra-articular corticosteroid is considered for persistent monoarthritis. Sulfasalazine or methotrexate is added if symptoms persist beyond 3-6 months.
Antibiotic courses do not change the natural history of post-enteric reactive arthritis; the inflammation is driven by immune cross-reactivity, not persistent organism (eTG).
DMARDs are reserved for reactive arthritis lasting beyond 3-6 months or with significant functional impact; first-line is NSAIDs (eTG).

Systemic steroids are not first-line for reactive arthritis; intra-articular steroid is preferred for persistent monoarthritis. Oral steroid is reserved for severe polyarthritis unresponsive to NSAIDs (eTG).
Urate is normal, the pattern is migratory inflammatory oligoarthritis with extra-articular features, and gout does not cause conjunctivitis or sterile dysuria. Allopurinol is not indicated (eTG).

explanation.summary: IRIS occurs when a recovering immune system mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response against previously subclinical or partially treated opportunistic infections. Unmasking IRIS reveals infections that were present but clinically silent at baseline. Risk factors include very low baseline CD4 count, high baseline viral load, and rapid virological suppression. Management involves continuing ART, treating the underlying opportunistic infection, and adding corticosteroids for severe inflammation.
key_points: IRIS typically occurs 2-8 weeks after ART initiation in patients with baseline CD4 below 100
Unmasking IRIS reveals subclinical infections; paradoxical IRIS worsens known infections
Confirmed by virological response plus new inflammatory presentation
ART should be continued; stopping ART worsens outcomes
explanation.pearls: The IRIS-associated mortality risk is highest with cryptococcal meningitis IRIS (up to 20-30%), while toxoplasma IRIS has a more favourable prognosis when treated with pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine alongside continued ART and short-course dexamethasone.

options.rationale: Treatment failure is excluded by the dramatic viral load decline from 320,000 to 800 copies per mL and CD4 rise from 42 to 145. Greater than 1 log reduction in viral load by 6 weeks confirms effective treatment. True failure would show stable or rising viral load. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

Primary CNS lymphoma typically presents with a single enhancing lesion and is more common at CD4 counts below 50. While ring enhancement can occur, the clinical context of rapid immune recovery on effective ART and toxoplasma seropositivity makes IRIS-associated toxoplasmosis far more likely. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: HIV)

PML typically presents with non-enhancing white matter lesions without mass effect on MRI, distinct from the ring-enhancing lesions with oedema seen here. PML also typically causes focal neurological deficits without fever. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

While cryptococcal meningitis is common at low CD4 counts, the imaging shows ring-enhancing parenchymal lesions rather than the basal meningeal enhancement typical of cryptococcal disease. The positive toxoplasma IgG and pattern of immune recovery favour IRIS-associated toxoplasmosis. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

The clinical picture is classic unmasking IRIS: a patient with very low baseline CD4 starts ART, achieves virological suppression with immune recovery, then develops paradoxical clinical deterioration 2-8 weeks into treatment. Ring-enhancing lesions with positive toxoplasma serology in a recovering immune system indicate IRIS-unmasked cerebral toxoplasmosis. IRIS occurs in 10-25% of patients starting ART at CD4 below 50. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection is not transmissible. The patient needs no isolation, no work exclusion and no contact tracing; she needs an explanation of why treatment is offered and which symptoms should bring her back.
key_points: Only active pulmonary or laryngeal disease is infectious.
Active tuberculosis is notifiable in NSW; latent infection is not.
Preventive treatment is offered to reduce a lifetime reactivation risk of roughly 5 to 10%.
explanation.context: The distinction between latent and active tuberculosis is the organising idea for the whole topic. A positive interferon gamma release assay or Mantoux test records an immune memory of exposure, nothing more: it cannot distinguish latent from active disease, does not indicate infectivity, and will stay positive after successful treatment, so it is never used to monitor response. Active disease is established by symptoms, imaging and microbiology. Once active disease is excluded, every downstream decision, from work restrictions to public health notification, follows from the fact that there are no transmissible organisms.

options.rationale: Latent infection means contained, non-replicating bacilli with no pulmonary cavitation and no cough, so there are no organisms to transmit. No work exclusion, isolation or contact tracing is required. (Source: NSW Health: Tuberculosis)

Work exclusion applies to smear positive pulmonary disease, where exclusion continues until clinical improvement and adequate treatment are documented with the treating unit. (Source: NSW Health: Tuberculosis)

Household contact screening is done when the index case has active pulmonary or laryngeal disease. Contact tracing follows the infectious case, not the person with latent infection. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee (NTAC) guidelines)

A negative sputum culture is required when active disease is being treated and infectivity must be documented as resolved. Sputum testing has no role once active disease has been excluded. (Source: NSW Health: Tuberculosis)
