A mask is worn by a person with suspected or confirmed infectious pulmonary disease before airborne precautions can be arranged. It implies a transmission risk that does not exist here. (Source: NSW Health: Tuberculosis)

explanation.summary: Peritoneal tuberculosis presents with ascites, constitutional symptoms, and peritoneal thickening. Key diagnostic clues include a low SAAG (exudative ascites), lymphocyte-predominant cell count, elevated ascitic fluid adenosine deaminase above 30-39 U/L, and necrotic lymphadenopathy on CT. CA-125 is commonly elevated and can mimic ovarian malignancy. Laparoscopic peritoneal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis. Treatment follows the standard 6-month RIPE regimen, though some centres extend to 9 months for peritoneal disease.
key_points: Peritoneal TB causes exudative ascites with low SAAG (< 11 g/L) and lymphocytic predominance
Ascitic fluid ADA > 30-39 U/L has approximately 90% sensitivity and specificity for TB
CA-125 elevation is common in peritoneal TB and may mislead toward ovarian malignancy
Laparoscopic peritoneal biopsy is the gold standard diagnostic investigation
explanation.pearls: Ascitic fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA) above 39 U/L has approximately 100% sensitivity and 97% specificity for peritoneal TB in high-prevalence populations, but specificity drops in cirrhotic patients where ADA may be elevated from other causes.

options.rationale: Peritoneal TB is a paucibacillary disease where ascitic fluid AFB smear and culture have low sensitivity (less than 20% for smear, 50-70% for culture). Laparoscopic peritoneal biopsy showing caseating granulomas on histology and positive mycobacterial culture is the gold standard for diagnosis. The characteristic laparoscopic appearance of miliary tubercles on the peritoneum is highly specific. Tissue culture also allows drug susceptibility testing. (Source: GESA Clinical Update; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This patient has no respiratory symptoms and a normal chest X-ray, making pulmonary TB unlikely. Sputum testing will not diagnose isolated peritoneal TB. While concurrent pulmonary disease should be excluded, the diagnostic priority is peritoneal tissue sampling. (Source: NTAC Guidelines)

While the clinical suspicion for peritoneal TB is high, empirical therapy without tissue diagnosis risks missing an alternative diagnosis (particularly ovarian malignancy, given the elevated CA-125 and peritoneal findings) and precludes drug susceptibility testing. Histological confirmation should be sought before committing to 6-12 months of therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

CT-guided FNA of a necrotic lymph node can yield useful material, but the diagnostic yield is lower than laparoscopic peritoneal biopsy for peritoneal TB. FNA provides limited tissue for histology compared to a full biopsy and may miss granulomas. Laparoscopy also allows direct visualisation of the peritoneum. (Source: GESA Clinical Update)

Ascitic fluid culture has a sensitivity of only 50-70% for peritoneal TB even with large volumes and mycobacterial culture. The high ascitic fluid ADA of 78 U/L already strongly supports the diagnosis, and repeating paracentesis is unlikely to change the diagnostic approach. Tissue biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis. (Source: GESA Clinical Update)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle and the Australian Sepsis Clinical Care Standard mandate prompt recognition of sepsis and initiation of treatment within 60 minutes. The bundle includes measuring lactate, obtaining blood cultures before antibiotics, administering broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, commencing IV fluid resuscitation with crystalloid, and applying vasopressors if hypotension persists despite fluids. Antibiotic administration is the single intervention with the strongest evidence for mortality reduction in sepsis.
key_points: IV antibiotics within 1 hour are the highest-impact intervention in sepsis
Each hour of antibiotic delay increases mortality by approximately 7-8%
Blood cultures should be obtained before antibiotics but must not delay antibiotic administration
Vasopressors are second-line after inadequate response to fluid resuscitation
explanation.pearls: The qSOFA score (altered mental status, RR >= 22, SBP <= 100 mmHg) identifies patients at higher risk of poor outcomes outside the ICU but should NOT delay the hour-1 bundle; in Australia, the between-the-flags early warning scores are used alongside clinical judgement for sepsis recognition.

options.rationale: Vasopressors are indicated for septic shock refractory to fluid resuscitation, but they are not the first priority. IV fluid resuscitation must be commenced first, and antibiotics are the single most time-critical intervention. Each hour of antibiotic delay in sepsis increases mortality by approximately 7-8%. (Source: Australian Sepsis Clinical Care Standard; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

The single most important intervention within the hour-1 sepsis bundle is the administration of appropriate IV antibiotics. In community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis, this would be IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin per eTG. Each hour of delay in antibiotic administration is associated with a 7-8% increase in mortality. While fluid resuscitation is also critical and should occur simultaneously, antibiotics are the intervention with the greatest impact on survival. (Source: Australian Sepsis Clinical Care Standard; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

The clinical picture is consistent with community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis. CTPA for PE is not indicated as first-line and would delay treatment. Investigations should not delay the hour-1 bundle. CT imaging may be considered later if the patient fails to respond to treatment. (Source: Australian Sepsis Clinical Care Standard)

Central venous catheter insertion is not a priority in the first hour of sepsis management. CVP-guided resuscitation has been shown to be no more effective than clinical assessment. The hour-1 bundle prioritises antibiotics, fluid resuscitation via peripheral access, and lactate measurement. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

IV hydrocortisone is recommended for septic shock refractory to fluids and vasopressors, not as a first-line intervention. It should only be considered after adequate fluid resuscitation and vasopressor initiation if shock persists. Early corticosteroids without vasopressor failure may cause harm. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Refractory septic shock is managed with a stepwise approach: adequate source control, appropriate antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, noradrenaline as the first-line vasopressor, vasopressin as the second-line vasopressor, and hydrocortisone for shock requiring escalating vasopressor doses. The ADRENAL trial (predominantly Australian and New Zealand ICUs) and APROCCHSS trial demonstrated that hydrocortisone 200 mg/day reduces time to shock resolution and may reduce mortality in severe septic shock. Bedside echocardiography guides the decision between vasopressor escalation and inotropic support.
key_points: Vasopressin (up to 0.03 units/min) is the recommended second vasopressor after noradrenaline
IV hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours for shock requiring escalating vasopressors
Echo-guided assessment distinguishes vasoplegic from cardiogenic shock
Dobutamine is reserved for sepsis-related cardiomyopathy with reduced cardiac output
explanation.pearls: The ADRENAL trial (3,658 patients across 69 Australian, NZ, UK, Saudi, and Danish ICUs) showed that IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day accelerated resolution of septic shock by approximately 1 day (median time to shock resolution 3 vs 4 days) but did not reduce 90-day mortality compared to placebo (27.9% vs 28.8%).

options.rationale: Escalating noradrenaline beyond 0.5 mcg/kg/min as monotherapy is associated with diminishing returns and increasing adverse effects including arrhythmias, peripheral ischaemia, and mesenteric vasoconstriction. Current guidelines recommend adding a second vasopressor rather than further escalating noradrenaline alone. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; ANZICS Guidelines)

Dobutamine is indicated for sepsis-related cardiomyopathy with reduced cardiac output. This patient has hyperdynamic LV function on echo, indicating adequate cardiac contractility. The shock is distributive (vasoplegic), not cardiogenic. Dobutamine would worsen tachycardia and hypotension through vasodilation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Switching to adrenaline as the sole vasopressor is not recommended. Adrenaline may be considered as a second-line vasopressor but is typically added to noradrenaline rather than replacing it. Adrenaline also causes hyperglycaemia and splanchnic vasoconstriction. The preferred second-line agent is vasopressin. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

While the IVC findings suggest some fluid responsiveness, 40 mL/kg has already been administered and further aggressive fluid loading risks pulmonary oedema and worsened organ function. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign suggests vasopressin addition rather than continued fluid loading in noradrenaline-refractory shock. Albumin may have a role but is not the priority intervention. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

For septic shock refractory to noradrenaline at 0.25-0.5 mcg/kg/min, the Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends adding vasopressin (up to 0.03 units/min) as the second vasopressor. Vasopressin acts via V1 receptors and is synergistic with catecholamines. IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg every 6 hours) is recommended for septic shock requiring escalating vasopressor support, as relative adrenal insufficiency is common in severe sepsis. The ADRENAL and APROCCHSS trials support this approach. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; ADRENAL Trial 2018; ANZICS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: HSV encephalitis is the most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis. It has a predilection for the temporal and frontal lobes, presenting with fever, behavioural change, seizures, and aphasia. MRI showing temporal lobe T2/FLAIR hyperintensity is highly characteristic. CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly elevated protein, normal or mildly reduced glucose, and occasionally red blood cells reflecting haemorrhagic necrosis. Treatment with IV aciclovir must commence immediately on clinical suspicion without awaiting CSF HSV PCR results.
key_points: Temporal lobe involvement on MRI with fever and behavioural change is classic for HSV encephalitis
IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly must start immediately - do not await PCR
CSF RBCs can be present due to haemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobe
Treatment duration is 14-21 days; repeat CSF PCR may guide duration
explanation.pearls: A negative CSF HSV PCR within the first 72 hours of symptom onset does not exclude HSV encephalitis, as PCR sensitivity is approximately 98% but may be falsely negative very early in the disease course; if clinical suspicion remains high, aciclovir should be continued and the LP repeated at 3-7 days.

options.rationale: Delaying aciclovir until HSV PCR results return is unacceptable. HSV encephalitis has a mortality exceeding 70% without treatment and approximately 20% with early treatment. PCR results take 24-48 hours, and each hour of delay worsens outcomes. Treatment must begin on clinical suspicion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Lancet Neurology HSV encephalitis review)

The clinical picture (temporal lobe involvement on MRI, behavioural change, seizure, lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose) is classic for HSV encephalitis, not bacterial meningitis. Bacterial meningitis typically shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, and meningeal signs. While empiric antibiotics may be given until bacterial infection is excluded, aciclovir for HSV encephalitis is the critical treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

The combination of fever, behavioural change, temporal lobe MRI changes, seizure, and lymphocytic CSF with mildly elevated protein and RBCs is classic for HSV encephalitis. IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly must be commenced immediately without waiting for PCR confirmation. Treatment duration is typically 14-21 days. Antiepileptic therapy (levetiracetam or valproate) should be commenced given the clinical seizure and temporal lobe inflammation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; IDSA Encephalitis Guidelines)

Oral valaciclovir does not achieve sufficient CSF concentrations for the treatment of HSV encephalitis. IV aciclovir is mandatory for CNS HSV infection. Oral valaciclovir is appropriate for mucocutaneous herpes and varicella zoster dermatomal disease but not for encephalitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AMH)

While autoimmune encephalitis is on the differential for temporal lobe encephalitis, the acute febrile onset with CSF RBCs and MRI showing temporal lobe swelling strongly favours HSV encephalitis. High-dose corticosteroids without antiviral cover in HSV encephalitis would be catastrophic. Autoimmune encephalitis is typically subacute and afebrile. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a rapidly progressive soft tissue infection involving the fascia and subcutaneous tissues with high mortality (20-40%). Key clinical features include pain out of proportion to visible changes, rapid progression despite antibiotics, haemorrhagic bullae, skin necrosis, crepitus, and systemic sepsis. Risk factors include diabetes, obesity, and immunosuppression. The definitive treatment is urgent surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Delay in surgery is the primary determinant of mortality.
key_points: Pain out of proportion to visible changes is the earliest and most important clinical sign
Subcutaneous gas and crepitus indicate gas-forming organisms but are not always present
Surgical debridement is definitive - antibiotics alone are insufficient
Do not delay surgery for imaging when the clinical diagnosis is clear
explanation.pearls: The LRINEC (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis) score uses CRP > 150 mg/L, WCC > 15 x10^9/L, Hb < 135 g/L, Na < 135 mmol/L, creatinine > 141 micromol/L, and glucose > 10 mmol/L; a score of 6 or more has approximately 92% positive predictive value, but clinical suspicion should override a low score.

sources.label: ANZCA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

options.rationale: Escalating antibiotics alone without surgical intervention is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis. While IV antibiotics are necessary, the defining treatment is urgent surgical debridement. Necrotising fasciitis cannot be cured with antibiotics alone due to thrombosis of nutrient vessels causing tissue necrosis beyond antibiotic reach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; eTG)

Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency. The key clinical features here are pain out of proportion to visible changes, rapid spread despite antibiotics, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, subcutaneous gas on X-ray, and sepsis. Urgent surgical debridement is the single most important intervention and should not be delayed for imaging. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin) and aggressive fluid resuscitation should be commenced simultaneously. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZCA/RACS Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines)
source_refs: ANZCA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

options.rationale: While MRI can identify fascial oedema and fluid tracking, imaging should not delay surgical exploration when the clinical diagnosis is strongly suspected. This patient has crepitus, subcutaneous gas on X-ray, and clinical sepsis. Surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic. MRI would cause dangerous delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Bedside incision and drainage is appropriate for a localised abscess but is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis, which requires extensive surgical debridement often involving large areas of tissue excision. The clinical features (pain disproportionate to appearance, crepitus, gas on X-ray, rapid spread, bullae) distinguish necrotising fasciitis from an abscess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Hyperbaric oxygen has been used as an adjunct in some centres for gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) but is not a substitute for surgical debridement. It should never delay surgery. Evidence for hyperbaric oxygen in necrotising fasciitis is limited and it is not standard first-line treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Bacterial meningitis in adults requires urgent empiric antibiotic therapy with IV dexamethasone. The de Gans trial demonstrated that dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. Standard empiric therapy is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin (for penicillin-resistant pneumococci). In patients over 50 years or immunocompromised, ampicillin is added for Listeria coverage. Lumbar puncture should not delay antibiotic administration if clinical suspicion is high.
key_points: IV dexamethasone must be given before or with the first dose of antibiotics to be effective
Empiric therapy: ceftriaxone 2 g BD + vancomycin; add ampicillin for Listeria cover if age >50 or immunocompromised
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV QID for 4 days reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis
CT brain before LP is indicated if there is reduced consciousness, focal neurology, papilloedema, or seizures
Do not delay antibiotics for LP - if LP cannot be performed within 30 minutes, give antibiotics and LP later
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone loses its mortality benefit if given more than 4 hours after the first antibiotic dose - the timing window is narrow, so it must be given concurrently with or immediately before antibiotics, not as an afterthought.

options.rationale: This combination provides appropriate antimicrobial coverage for bacterial meningitis (ceftriaxone for Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae, vancomycin for penicillin-resistant pneumococci). However, it omits dexamethasone, which should be given before or with the first dose of antibiotics to reduce mortality and neurological sequelae from pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Benzylpenicillin alone does not provide adequate empiric coverage for bacterial meningitis in adults. It does not cover penicillin-resistant pneumococci and achieves inadequate CSF concentrations against some organisms. Empiric therapy should include a third-generation cephalosporin. Benzylpenicillin monotherapy may be used pre-hospital as an initial dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This combination is used for Listeria monocytogenes meningitis coverage, which is typically added for patients over 50 years, immunocompromised, or pregnant. While this patient is 55, the combination lacks coverage for penicillin-resistant pneumococci and does not include dexamethasone. Listeria cover would be added to ceftriaxone, not used as the sole regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Fluconazole targets fungal meningitis (Cryptococcus), which presents subacutely over weeks, typically in immunocompromised patients. This acute presentation with high fever, meningism, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers in an immunocompetent patient is consistent with bacterial meningitis. Fungal cover is not appropriate as empiric first-line therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

For suspected bacterial meningitis in adults, Australian guidelines recommend IV dexamethasone 10 mg given immediately before or with the first dose of antibiotics, followed by ceftriaxone and vancomycin. Dexamethasone reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis. At age 55, empiric benzylpenicillin or ampicillin should also be considered for Listeria cover, but the critical point is that dexamethasone must accompany the antibiotics. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: DOACs are now first-line for uncomplicated DVT and PE in most patients. Rivaroxaban and apixaban can be started without parenteral heparin lead-in (they have their own loading dose regimens), while dabigatran and edoxaban require 5 days of parenteral heparin first. For provoked DVT with a clear transient risk factor (surgery, immobilisation, long-haul travel), 3 months of anticoagulation is standard. Unprovoked DVT may require extended or indefinite anticoagulation based on bleeding risk assessment.
key_points: Rivaroxaban and apixaban do not require parenteral heparin lead-in
Rivaroxaban loading: 15 mg BD for 21 days, then 20 mg daily
Provoked DVT with transient risk factor: 3 months anticoagulation
DOACs are preferred over warfarin for uncomplicated VTE in patients with normal renal function
Dabigatran and edoxaban require 5 days of parenteral heparin before commencing
explanation.pearls: Rivaroxaban's 21-day loading phase (15 mg BD) provides intensified anticoagulation during the highest-risk period for clot extension, then steps down to 20 mg daily - missing this loading phase risks treatment failure.

options.rationale: Warfarin was the traditional standard of care for VTE but requires bridging with parenteral heparin, regular INR monitoring, and has significant food and drug interactions. DOACs are now preferred first-line for uncomplicated provoked DVT due to equivalent efficacy, lower bleeding risk, and ease of use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

This is the traditional heparin-bridging-to-warfarin approach. While effective, DOACs are preferred for uncomplicated VTE as they eliminate the need for heparin bridging (with rivaroxaban and apixaban) and INR monitoring. This approach is now reserved for situations where DOACs are contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Aspirin has a modest effect on VTE recurrence prevention but is markedly inferior to anticoagulation. It is not recommended as the sole treatment for acute DVT. Aspirin may have a role as extended secondary prevention after completing the anticoagulation course for unprovoked VTE, but not as initial therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Rivaroxaban is a DOAC approved for acute DVT treatment. The regimen is 15 mg twice daily for the first 21 days (loading phase) followed by 20 mg once daily. For a provoked DVT with a clear transient risk factor (long-haul flight), the recommended duration is 3 months. Rivaroxaban does not require heparin lead-in, is taken orally from the start, and has equivalent efficacy to conventional therapy with lower major bleeding risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Dabigatran is an effective DOAC for VTE but requires a mandatory 5-day lead-in with parenteral heparin before starting oral dabigatran. This adds complexity compared to rivaroxaban or apixaban, which can be started without parenteral heparin. Both approaches are effective, but rivaroxaban or apixaban monotherapy is preferred when simplicity is a priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: VTE treatment has an initial phase of at least 3 months, then a decision about extended therapy that turns on whether the event was provoked and on bleeding risk. PE provoked by a major transient factor such as surgery is treated for 3 months; unprovoked PE with a low bleeding risk is usually treated indefinitely. Extended therapy can step down to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily after 6 months. Aspirin is a weak substitute kept for patients who cannot take anticoagulation.
key_points: All patients with PE receive at least 3 months of anticoagulation.
Unprovoked PE with low bleeding risk: extended anticoagulation without a planned stop date.
After 6 months, rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is as efficacious as full dose for extended prevention.
Aspirin is avoided for extended VTE prevention unless anticoagulation cannot be used.
explanation.pearls: HERDOO2 identifies women with a first unprovoked VTE who can stop anticoagulation after short-term treatment; REVERSE II validated it in women only.

sources.label: Rodger MA et al. HERDOO2 validation (REVERSE II), BMJ 2017

options.rationale: After an unprovoked PE, THANZ advises deciding at 3 months whether to stop or continue with extended therapy, and a low bleeding risk favours continuing without a planned stop date, with regular review of bleeding risk, renal function and adherence. From 6 months, THANZ notes rivaroxaban 10 mg daily is as efficacious as 20 mg daily, so a dose reduction is an option then. (Source: THANZ VTE guideline (MJA 2019); Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

THANZ sets at least 3 months of anticoagulation for all proximal DVT and PE. Stopping at 3 months suits PE provoked by a major transient risk factor such as surgery, where the recurrence risk falls once the trigger has passed. (Source: THANZ VTE guideline (MJA 2019))

THANZ advises that aspirin be avoided for extended VTE prevention unless anticoagulation cannot be used, for example after a major bleed on anticoagulation or when the patient declines it. (Source: THANZ VTE guideline (MJA 2019))

D-dimer-guided stopping leaves him unprotected while the test is done, and the validated HERDOO2 rule for stopping after unprovoked VTE applies to women only. The extended-therapy decision for him rests on recurrence against bleeding risk. (Source: Rodger MA et al. HERDOO2 validation (REVERSE II), BMJ 2017; THANZ VTE guideline (MJA 2019))
source_refs: Rodger MA et al. HERDOO2 validation (REVERSE II), BMJ 2017

options.rationale: A fixed extra 3 months delays the stop-or-continue decision THANZ places at 3 months without changing the answer for an unprovoked PE with low bleeding risk. A time-limited course with a planned stop suits PE provoked by a transient risk factor. (Source: THANZ VTE guideline (MJA 2019))

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in young, tall, thin individuals without underlying lung disease. Management depends on size and symptoms. Small asymptomatic pneumothorax can be observed. Symptomatic or moderate-to-large pneumothorax (>2 cm on chest X-ray) is managed with needle aspiration as first-line. Chest drain insertion follows failed aspiration. Recurrent pneumothorax or persistent air leak warrants surgical referral for VATS and pleurodesis.
key_points: Needle aspiration is first-line for symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax >2 cm
Small (<2 cm) asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax can be observed
If aspiration fails (lung does not re-expand), insert a small-bore intercostal drain
Surgical referral (VATS pleurodesis) is for recurrent episodes, persistent air leak, or bilateral pneumothorax
Supplemental oxygen accelerates reabsorption but does not replace active intervention for larger pneumothoraces
explanation.pearls: Needle aspiration for primary spontaneous pneumothorax has an immediate success rate of approximately 60-80% - if the first attempt fails (>2.5 L aspirated without resistance or lung fails to re-expand), a second attempt is not recommended; proceed to intercostal drain.

options.rationale: Observation alone is appropriate for small primary spontaneous pneumothorax (less than 2 cm from the chest wall or less than 1 cm at the apex). This pneumothorax is moderate (3 cm from the chest wall at the hilum) and the patient is symptomatic, warranting active intervention with needle aspiration as the first step. (Source: BTS: Pneumothorax Guidelines)

For a symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax larger than 2 cm, needle aspiration is the recommended first-line intervention. A 16-18G cannula is inserted in the second intercostal space, midclavicular line (or safe triangle) with aspiration of air using a syringe and three-way tap. If successful (lung re-expands on repeat X-ray), the patient can be discharged with outpatient follow-up. If aspiration fails, an intercostal catheter is the next step. (Source: BTS: Pneumothorax Guidelines)

A large-bore intercostal drain (chest tube) is not first-line for primary spontaneous pneumothorax. It is more invasive, more painful, and associated with longer hospital stays than needle aspiration. Current guidelines recommend aspiration as the first intervention, with chest drain insertion reserved for failed aspiration or secondary pneumothorax. Small-bore drains (10-14F) are preferred over large-bore when drainage is needed. (Source: BTS: Pneumothorax Guidelines)

Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with pleurodesis is reserved for recurrent pneumothorax, persistent air leak beyond 5-7 days, bilateral pneumothorax, or high-risk occupations. A first episode of primary spontaneous pneumothorax is managed conservatively with aspiration or drainage. Surgical referral at this stage is premature. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Supplemental oxygen can accelerate pneumothorax reabsorption (by approximately 4-fold) by reducing the partial pressure of nitrogen in the blood. However, high-flow oxygen alone is not the primary intervention for a moderate symptomatic pneumothorax. It can be used as an adjunct alongside aspiration but does not replace the need for active air removal. (Source: BTS: Pneumothorax Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Light's criteria distinguish transudative from exudative pleural effusions using three biochemical parameters. An effusion is exudative if any one criterion is met: pleural/serum protein ratio >0.5, pleural/serum LDH ratio >0.6, or pleural LDH > two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Transudative effusions are caused by systemic factors (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), while exudative effusions result from local processes (infection, malignancy, inflammation). Light's criteria have 98% sensitivity for exudates but may misclassify some transudates in diuretic-treated heart failure patients.
key_points: Light's criteria: protein ratio >0.5 OR LDH ratio >0.6 OR pleural LDH > two-thirds ULN for serum LDH
Any ONE criterion positive = exudate; all three negative = transudate
Common transudative causes: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
Common exudative causes: infection, malignancy, PE, autoimmune disease
Diuretics can concentrate transudates, causing misclassification as exudates - check serum-pleural albumin gradient if suspected
explanation.pearls: Light's criteria misclassify approximately 25% of heart failure transudates as exudates in patients on diuretics - if clinical suspicion for transudate is high despite meeting exudative criteria, a serum-to-pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L confirms a true transudate.

options.rationale: The pleural fluid to serum protein ratio is 22/62 = 0.35, which is below the 0.5 threshold for an exudate. All three Light's criteria must be checked, and at least one must be met to classify an effusion as exudative. This ratio does not meet the exudative criterion. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pleural Effusion)

The pleural fluid to serum LDH ratio is 85/180 = 0.47, which is below the 0.6 threshold for an exudate. This criterion is not met. An exudate requires at least one of three criteria to be positive: protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, or pleural fluid LDH above two-thirds the upper limit of serum normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Light's criteria classify an effusion as exudative if ANY one of three criteria is met: (1) pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5 (22/62 = 0.35 - not met), (2) pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6 (85/180 = 0.47 - not met), (3) pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds upper limit of normal serum LDH (if ULN = 250, threshold = 167; 85 < 167 - not met). As none are met, this is a transudate, consistent with heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Glucose levels in pleural fluid can help identify complicated effusions (parapneumonic, empyema, rheumatoid, malignancy) when markedly low (<3.3 mmol/L), but glucose is not part of Light's criteria for classification. The glucose here is 5.8 mmol/L which is normal and does not indicate an exudate or a complicated effusion. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pleural Effusion)

Light's criteria provide definitive classification in the vast majority of cases. 'Indeterminate' is not a Light's criteria category. The criteria are binary: if at least one criterion is met, the effusion is exudative; if none are met, it is transudative. Pleural biopsy is reserved for undiagnosed exudative effusions, particularly when malignancy or tuberculosis is suspected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea is diagnosed by polysomnography, which measures the apnoea-hypopnoea index. OSA severity is graded by AHI: mild (5-15), moderate (15-30), severe (>30). Risk factors include obesity, large neck circumference (>40 cm women, >43 cm men), crowded oropharynx, retrognathia, and male sex. OSA is an important cause of resistant hypertension. CPAP is the first-line treatment for moderate-to-severe OSA and can improve blood pressure control, daytime sleepiness, and cardiovascular outcomes.
key_points: Polysomnography is the gold-standard diagnostic investigation for OSA
AHI severity grading: mild 5-15, moderate 15-30, severe >30 events per hour
CPAP is first-line treatment for moderate-to-severe OSA
OSA is present in up to 80% of patients with resistant hypertension
Epworth Sleepiness Scale >10 suggests excessive daytime sleepiness warranting investigation
explanation.pearls: Resistant hypertension (uncontrolled BP despite three antihypertensives including a diuretic) should trigger screening for OSA - treating the OSA with CPAP can reduce systolic blood pressure by 5-10 mmHg and may allow medication reduction.

options.rationale: Overnight pulse oximetry can detect cyclical desaturation patterns suggestive of OSA but has limited sensitivity (approximately 60-70%) and cannot quantify the apnoea-hypopnoea index or distinguish obstructive from central events. Given the high pre-test probability in this patient, a more definitive investigation is warranted. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

Cephalometric X-ray can identify anatomical contributors to OSA (retrognathia, macroglossia, reduced posterior airway space) but is not a diagnostic test for OSA. It may be useful pre-operatively if maxillomandibular advancement surgery is being considered, but the priority is confirming the diagnosis and quantifying severity with a sleep study. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

CT of the neck is not part of the routine diagnostic pathway for OSA. The clinical history and examination already identify significant risk factors (obesity, large neck, crowded oropharynx, retrognathia). Structural imaging is not needed before proceeding to a sleep study unless a specific structural lesion (tumour, goitre) is suspected. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

ABG can identify chronic hypercapnia (obesity hypoventilation syndrome) which may coexist with OSA. However, it does not diagnose OSA itself and should not delay the sleep study. ABG is indicated if there is clinical suspicion of obesity hypoventilation (daytime hypercapnia, polycythaemia) but is not the first investigation for OSA. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

Polysomnography (in-laboratory or home-based level 2-3 study) is the gold-standard investigation for diagnosing and grading OSA severity. It measures the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI), which guides management: mild (5-15), moderate (15-30), severe (>30). This patient has a high clinical probability of moderate-to-severe OSA (ESS 16, witnessed apnoeas, resistant hypertension, obesity, large neck), and the AHI will determine CPAP eligibility. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

explanation.summary: Internal carotid artery dissection classically presents with constant unilateral head, face or neck pain and an ipsilateral partial Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis with preserved facial sweating, since the sudomotor fibres travel with the external carotid), often after trivial neck strain, sport or manipulation. Cluster headache is the main mimic but gives discrete attacks of 15 to 180 minutes with prominent lacrimation, rhinorrhoea and agitated restlessness, and any Horner syndrome resolves between bouts. CT or MR angiography of the head and neck makes the diagnosis, and antithrombotic treatment is started to prevent embolic stroke, which is the reason for urgency. In context: a first severe headache with a new neurological sign is investigated rather than treated symptomatically, whatever the pain pattern looks like.
key_points: Constant pain plus a new partial Horner syndrome means dissection until imaged
Cluster headache gives episodic attacks, marked autonomic tearing and restlessness
CT or MR angiography of head and neck is the diagnostic test; plain CT does not exclude it
The risk being prevented is embolic stroke in the following days
explanation.pearls: The Horner syndrome of carotid dissection spares sweating because the sudomotor fibres to the face run with the external carotid artery, which distinguishes it from a preganglionic lesion.

options.rationale: Constant unilateral head and neck pain with a partial Horner syndrome after exertion is internal carotid artery dissection until proven otherwise, and angiography is needed before stroke occurs. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

Oxygen aborts cluster headache, which gives discrete attacks of 15 to 180 minutes with lacrimation and restlessness, and no Horner syndrome between attacks. His pain is continuous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Non-contrast CT is the first test for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with thunderclap onset. It does not exclude dissection, so a normal scan would falsely reassure. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

Verapamil prevents cluster headache once that diagnosis is established in a patient with a typical bout of short stereotyped attacks. Starting it here delays imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
A triptan aborts migraine and cluster attacks. Giving a vasoconstrictor in possible dissection is unsafe, and a week of delay is where the stroke happens. (Source: AMH: Sumatriptan)

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease. Treatment indications include symptomatic pulmonary disease with impaired lung function, hypercalcaemia, cardiac involvement, neurological involvement, and significant eye or skin disease not responding to topical therapy. Oral corticosteroids are first-line, with steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate) added for refractory disease or intolerable steroid side effects. Erythema nodosum in sarcoidosis is part of Lofgren syndrome and may respond to NSAIDs alone, but this patient has additional treatment indications.
key_points: Oral prednisolone is first-line treatment when sarcoidosis treatment is indicated
Treatment indications: symptomatic lung disease with reduced FVC/DLCO, hypercalcaemia, cardiac/neuro involvement
Hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis is due to 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in granulomas converting 25-OH vitamin D to calcitriol
Steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, azathioprine) are second-line for refractory disease
Asymptomatic bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (stage I) without organ dysfunction can be observed
explanation.pearls: Sarcoidosis-related hypercalcaemia is driven by unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase in granulomas - it responds rapidly to corticosteroids and patients should avoid vitamin D supplementation and excessive sun exposure during active disease.

options.rationale: While pulmonary sarcoidosis with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy alone (Scadding stage I-II) often resolves spontaneously, this patient has treatment indications: hypercalcaemia (2.78 mmol/L), reduced DLCO (65%), reduced FVC (72%), and symptomatic disease. Observation would be appropriate only for asymptomatic stage I disease without organ dysfunction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Oral corticosteroids are first-line treatment for sarcoidosis when treatment is indicated. Indications include symptomatic pulmonary disease with reduced lung function, hypercalcaemia, and significant extrapulmonary involvement. Starting dose is typically prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day (approximately 30 mg/day) for 4-6 weeks, then gradual taper over 6-12 months guided by symptoms and lung function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Methotrexate is an effective steroid-sparing agent in sarcoidosis but is second-line, used when corticosteroids cannot be tapered adequately or when steroid side effects are unacceptable. First-line treatment for newly diagnosed sarcoidosis requiring therapy is oral prednisolone. Methotrexate may be added after 3-6 months if steroid tapering proves difficult. (Source: BTS: Sarcoidosis Guidelines)

Inhaled corticosteroids have limited evidence in pulmonary sarcoidosis. They may provide modest benefit for cough as a symptom but do not adequately treat the granulomatous inflammation, improve lung function, or address the hypercalcaemia. Systemic corticosteroids are needed for the degree of disease in this patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Hydroxychloroquine is useful for cutaneous sarcoidosis and arthralgias but does not adequately treat pulmonary sarcoidosis or hypercalcaemia. This patient has significant pulmonary involvement (reduced FVC and DLCO) and hypercalcaemia that require systemic corticosteroids. Hydroxychloroquine may be considered as an adjunct for the erythema nodosum specifically. (Source: BTS: Sarcoidosis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive fibrosing interstitial lung disease with a median survival of 3-5 years from diagnosis. The UIP pattern on HRCT (basal honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, minimal ground glass opacity) is diagnostic when clinical context is consistent and autoimmune serology is negative. Antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone and nintedanib) are the standard of care and slow FVC decline. Corticosteroids and immunosuppressants are harmful in IPF. Lung transplantation should be considered for eligible patients.
key_points: UIP pattern on HRCT: basal honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, subpleural distribution, minimal GGO
Antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone or nintedanib) slow FVC decline by approximately 50%
Corticosteroids and immunosuppressants are harmful in IPF (PANTHER trial)
PBS eligibility for antifibrotics requires FVC 50-80% predicted in Australia
Lung transplantation referral should be considered early in the disease course
explanation.pearls: The DLCO is often the earliest and most disproportionately reduced lung function parameter in IPF - a DLCO below 40% predicted identifies patients at highest risk of mortality and should prompt urgent transplant referral.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not effective for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (or usual interstitial pneumonia pattern) and may cause harm. The PANTHER trial showed that corticosteroids combined with azathioprine and N-acetylcysteine increased mortality in IPF. Corticosteroids are indicated for inflammatory ILDs (sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, NSIP) but not for established fibrosis with honeycombing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Immunosuppression with azathioprine is used for autoimmune-related ILDs (connective tissue disease-associated ILD, sarcoidosis) but is contraindicated in IPF. The PANTHER trial demonstrated increased mortality with the combination of prednisolone, azathioprine, and N-acetylcysteine in IPF. This patient's autoimmune serology is negative. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

The UIP (usual interstitial pneumonia) pattern on HRCT with honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, basal predominance, and negative autoimmune serology is diagnostic of IPF (or possibly asbestosis given the occupational history, but managed identically). Antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone or nintedanib) slow the rate of FVC decline by approximately 50% and are the standard of care. Both are PBS-listed in Australia for IPF with FVC 50-80% predicted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Pulmonary hypertension can complicate advanced IPF, and sildenafil has been studied in this context. However, the STEP-IPF trial showed no significant benefit of sildenafil for IPF-associated pulmonary hypertension, and it is not recommended as primary treatment. Antifibrotic therapy to slow disease progression is the priority. (Source: NICE NG147: IPF)

N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was previously used in IPF based on its antioxidant properties. However, the PANTHER trial showed no benefit of NAC monotherapy in IPF, and the combination arm (NAC + prednisolone + azathioprine) showed harm. NAC is no longer recommended for IPF treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Migraine prophylaxis is indicated when attacks occur 4 or more days per month, significantly impact function, or when acute medication is overused (triptans >10 days/month, simple analgesics >15 days/month). First-line prophylactics include propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, and candesartan. The choice is guided by comorbidities and contraindications. In women planning pregnancy, topiramate and valproate are contraindicated. In asthma, beta-blockers are contraindicated. Amitriptyline is the best option when both constraints apply.
key_points: Migraine prophylaxis is indicated for 4+ headache days/month or acute medication overuse
Propranolol is contraindicated in asthma
Topiramate and valproate are contraindicated in women planning pregnancy
Amitriptyline 10-50 mg nocte is safe in asthma and has acceptable pregnancy safety profile
Triptan use >10 days/month suggests medication overuse headache - prophylaxis helps reduce acute medication use
explanation.pearls: Medication overuse headache should be suspected when acute migraine treatments are used more than 10 days per month for triptans or 15 days per month for simple analgesics - starting prophylaxis allows reduction of acute medication use, which itself improves headache frequency.

options.rationale: Propranolol is a first-line migraine prophylactic and is effective. However, it is contraindicated in this patient with asthma - beta-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm in asthmatic patients. Even cardioselective beta-blockers carry some risk. An alternative first-line agent should be chosen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Topiramate is an effective migraine prophylactic. However, it is teratogenic (FDA category D) and absolutely contraindicated in women planning pregnancy. It is associated with increased risk of cleft lip and palate, and requires reliable contraception during use. Since this patient is planning pregnancy within 12 months, topiramate is not appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Sodium valproate is effective for migraine prophylaxis but is a known teratogen with significant risks of neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental impairment. It is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential planning pregnancy. Australian guidelines recommend avoiding valproate in any woman who could become pregnant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Amitriptyline is a first-line migraine prophylactic that is safe in asthma (unlike propranolol) and has a relatively favourable safety profile in pregnancy (category C - used when benefits outweigh risks, with extensive clinical experience). Starting dose is 10 mg nocte, titrating to 25-50 mg. It is also useful if there is comorbid tension-type headache or insomnia. The frequency of 10 headache days per month and triptan overuse both indicate prophylaxis is needed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

CGRP monoclonal antibodies (galcanezumab, fremanezumab, erenumab) are effective for migraine prophylaxis and are PBS-listed in Australia for chronic migraine (>=15 headache days/month) after failing two prior prophylactics. This patient has episodic migraine (10 days/month) and has not yet trialled first-line prophylaxis. CGRP antibodies are also not recommended in pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke with large vessel occlusion requires a combined approach: IV thrombolysis (tenecteplase preferred for LVO in Australia) at the presenting hospital followed by urgent transfer for endovascular thrombectomy. The CT perfusion mismatch (small core, large penumbra) confirms salvageable tissue. Thrombectomy has been shown to improve outcomes up to 24 hours from onset when perfusion imaging demonstrates a target mismatch. The drip-and-ship model enables thrombolysis at regional centres with transfer to comprehensive stroke centres for thrombectomy.
key_points: Tenecteplase is now preferred over alteplase for large vessel occlusion stroke in Australia
Thrombectomy is indicated for LVO with NIHSS >=6 and favourable perfusion imaging
Drip-and-ship model: thrombolyse locally, transfer urgently for thrombectomy
BP target for thrombolysis eligibility is <185/110 mmHg, not <140/90
CT perfusion mismatch (small core, large penumbra) identifies patients who benefit from thrombectomy up to 24 hours
explanation.pearls: The EXTEND-IA TNK trial conducted in Australia demonstrated that tenecteplase achieved higher rates of MCA reperfusion before thrombectomy than alteplase (22% vs 10%), supporting its use as the preferred thrombolytic in the drip-and-ship pathway.

options.rationale: IV alteplase (thrombolysis) should be given if within the 4.5-hour window, but current Australian Stroke Foundation guidelines recommend tenecteplase as the preferred thrombolytic for large vessel occlusion stroke due to its single-bolus administration, higher recanalisation rate, and logistical advantages. However, the key point is that thrombolysis should not delay transfer for thrombectomy. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines)

Conservative management with antiplatelets alone would result in a poor outcome for this patient with a large vessel occlusion and NIHSS of 18. The CT perfusion shows a large salvageable penumbra (120 mL) with a small core (15 mL), indicating significant tissue at risk that could be saved with reperfusion. Thrombectomy is strongly indicated. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines)

IV heparin is not indicated in acute ischaemic stroke management. Anticoagulation for the underlying atrial fibrillation will be commenced after the acute phase (typically 4-14 days post-stroke depending on infarct size). The immediate priority is reperfusion therapy: thrombolysis plus thrombectomy for this large vessel occlusion. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines)

The BP target before thrombolysis is <185/110 mmHg, not <140/90. This patient's BP of 172/94 is already below the thrombolysis threshold and does not require reduction. Aggressive BP lowering to <140/90 in acute ischaemic stroke may worsen ischaemia by reducing perfusion to the penumbra. Time to treatment is critical and should not be delayed for unnecessary BP management. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines)

This patient meets criteria for both thrombolysis (within 4.5 hours, no contraindications) and thrombectomy (large vessel occlusion, NIHSS >=6, small core with large penumbra mismatch). Australian guidelines now recommend tenecteplase over alteplase for large vessel occlusion. The drip-and-ship model (thrombolyse locally, transfer for thrombectomy) is appropriate when the nearest comprehensive stroke centre is hours away. Transfer should not be delayed for post-thrombolysis observation. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Blood pressure management after thrombolysis for ischaemic stroke follows strict protocols. The target is <180/105 mmHg for the first 24 hours to minimise haemorrhagic transformation risk while maintaining adequate cerebral perfusion. This is stricter than the non-thrombolysed target (<220/120). Frequent BP monitoring is essential. After 24 hours, gradual introduction of oral antihypertensives is appropriate. Long-term BP control to <130/80 reduces recurrent stroke risk.
key_points: Post-thrombolysis BP target: <180/105 mmHg for the first 24 hours
Non-thrombolysed ischaemic stroke: permissive hypertension up to 220/120 mmHg
Frequent monitoring: every 15 min for 2 hours, then every 30 min for 6 hours, then hourly
IV labetalol, hydralazine, or glyceryl trinitrate infusion for acute BP management
After 24 hours without haemorrhage, gradually commence oral antihypertensives
explanation.pearls: The BP target after thrombolysis (<180/105) is 40 mmHg systolic lower than the non-thrombolysed target (<220/120) - this reflects the increased haemorrhagic transformation risk after thrombolysis, which rises approximately 6% for every 10 mmHg increase in systolic BP above 180.

options.rationale: After IV thrombolysis for ischaemic stroke, blood pressure should be maintained below 180/105 mmHg for the first 24 hours to reduce the risk of symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage. This is the standard post-thrombolysis BP target. Frequent monitoring (every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours, then every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly for 16 hours) is required. IV labetalol or hydralazine are common choices for acute BP management. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines)

Aggressive BP reduction to <140/90 in the first 24 hours post-thrombolysis is not recommended and may worsen outcomes. The ischaemic penumbra relies on collateral perfusion, which is pressure-dependent. Rapid lowering below 140/90 may extend the infarct. The ENCHANTED trial showed no benefit of intensive BP lowering to <140 mmHg systolic after thrombolysis. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines)

Permissive hypertension up to 220/120 mmHg is the approach for ischaemic stroke patients who have NOT received thrombolysis. Once thrombolysis has been administered, the BP target is stricter (<180/105) because hypertension increases the risk of haemorrhagic transformation of the thrombolysed tissue. (Source: AHA/ASA Stroke Guidelines)

GTN patches were studied in the RIGHT-2 and ENOS trials for acute stroke BP management. Neither showed benefit from acute BP lowering in the first 48 hours of stroke. A target of 120-130 mmHg systolic is too aggressive in the acute post-thrombolysis period and risks worsening ischaemia. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines)

While avoiding excessive BP lowering is important, completely withholding antihypertensives when BP exceeds the post-thrombolysis threshold of 180/105 is inappropriate. The current BP of 178/96 is just below the threshold and may exceed it, requiring treatment. Active monitoring with PRN antihypertensive to maintain <180/105 is the correct approach. (Source: AHA/ASA Stroke Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Cancer-associated VTE is treated with anticoagulation for at least 6 months and continued as long as cancer is active or treatment is ongoing. DOACs (apixaban and rivaroxaban) are now first-line for most cancer-associated VTE, replacing LMWH as the standard of care. The exception is high GI bleeding risk from luminal GI malignancies (oesophageal, gastric, small bowel, colorectal) where LMWH may be preferred. Warfarin is inferior to both DOACs and LMWH in cancer patients.
key_points: DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) are first-line for most cancer-associated VTE
LMWH is preferred over DOACs for luminal GI malignancies with high GI bleeding risk
Treatment duration: at least 6 months, continued while cancer is active or on treatment
Warfarin is inferior to both DOACs and LMWH for cancer-associated VTE
IVC filters are only for patients with absolute contraindications to anticoagulation
explanation.pearls: The Caravaggio trial specifically included pancreatic cancer patients and showed no excess GI bleeding with apixaban vs dalteparin - this distinguishes it from the SELECT-D trial where rivaroxaban showed higher bleeding in upper GI cancers, making apixaban the generally preferred DOAC for cancer-associated VTE.

options.rationale: Warfarin is inferior to both LMWH and DOACs for cancer-associated VTE. The CLOT trial demonstrated that dalteparin reduced VTE recurrence by 52% compared to warfarin in cancer patients. Warfarin also has significant drug interactions with chemotherapy agents and variable absorption in patients with GI malignancies or mucositis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

DOACs (apixaban and rivaroxaban specifically) are now recommended first-line for cancer-associated VTE in patients without high GI bleeding risk. The Caravaggio trial demonstrated non-inferiority of apixaban to dalteparin for cancer-associated VTE with similar major bleeding rates. Pancreatic cancer was not associated with excess GI bleeding with apixaban in this trial. Treatment should continue for at least 6 months and as long as cancer is active or chemotherapy continues. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

LMWH (enoxaparin or dalteparin) was the previous standard of care for cancer-associated VTE. However, the SELECT-D and Caravaggio trials demonstrated that DOACs (rivaroxaban and apixaban) are non-inferior with comparable safety. DOACs are preferred for patient convenience (oral administration, no injections) unless there is a high GI bleeding risk from a luminal GI malignancy. (Source: ISTH: Cancer-Associated VTE)

Rivaroxaban is an acceptable DOAC for cancer-associated VTE. However, the SELECT-D trial showed a higher rate of clinically relevant non-major bleeding with rivaroxaban compared to dalteparin, particularly in upper GI malignancies. For pancreatic cancer, apixaban (Caravaggio trial data) demonstrated a more favourable safety profile. Both are reasonable but apixaban is generally preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

IVC filters are reserved for patients with acute VTE who have absolute contraindications to anticoagulation (active major bleeding, very severe thrombocytopenia). This patient has no contraindication to anticoagulation. IVC filters do not treat existing DVT, carry their own thrombotic complications, and should be retrieved once anticoagulation can be commenced. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Australian CAP management uses the SMART-COP tool to stratify severity and guide antibiotic choice and disposition. SMART-COP predicts the need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support. Low-severity (0-2 points): oral amoxicillin, outpatient. Moderate (3-4): oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline, hospital ward. Severe (>=5): IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, consider ICU. SMART-COP parameters include systolic BP, multilobar involvement, albumin, respiratory rate, tachycardia, confusion, oxygen, and pH.
key_points: SMART-COP stratifies CAP severity: 0-2 mild, 3-4 moderate, >=5 severe
Moderate CAP: oral amoxicillin 1 g TDS plus doxycycline 100 mg BD (or azithromycin)
Severe CAP: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus azithromycin 500 mg daily
Duration of antibiotics for uncomplicated CAP is 5 days (review at 48-72 hours)
Atypical cover (doxycycline or macrolide) is added for moderate and severe CAP
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP was developed in Australia specifically for CAP and predicts ICU admission better than CURB-65 or PSI - the oxygen component (PaO2 <70 mmHg or SpO2 <=93% on room air) earns 2 points and is the most heavily weighted parameter.

options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin monotherapy is appropriate for low-severity CAP (SMART-COP 0-2) managed in the community. This patient has moderate-severity pneumonia: SpO2 94%, respiratory rate 22, and PaO2 68 mmHg suggest he is borderline for hospital admission. SMART-COP scoring indicates he may benefit from inpatient management with broader empiric coverage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

IV ceftriaxone plus a macrolide is appropriate for severe CAP requiring ICU admission or SMART-COP score >=5 (high risk of requiring intensive respiratory or vasopressor support). This patient's presentation is moderate, not severe - his SMART-COP score is approximately 2-3 (SpO2 <=93 earns 2 points, RR >=25 would earn 1). Moderate CAP does not routinely require IV combination therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

For moderate-severity CAP requiring hospital admission (SMART-COP 3-4), Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend oral amoxicillin 1 g TDS plus doxycycline 100 mg BD (or a macrolide) to cover both typical (Streptococcus pneumoniae) and atypical (Mycoplasma, Legionella) organisms. This patient's SpO2 of 94% and PaO2 of 68 mmHg warrant admission but not ICU-level therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Piperacillin-tazobactam provides broad Gram-negative and anaerobic cover and is not first-line for community-acquired pneumonia. It is reserved for hospital-acquired pneumonia, aspiration pneumonia with significant anaerobic risk, or when Pseudomonas coverage is specifically required (e.g. structural lung disease, recent hospitalisation). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Respiratory fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin, levofloxacin) have a role in CAP in some international guidelines, but ciprofloxacin has poor pneumococcal coverage and is not appropriate for CAP. Australian guidelines do not recommend fluoroquinolones as first-line for CAP due to resistance concerns and the availability of effective alternatives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients with underlying lung disease (COPD, CF, ILD) and is more dangerous than primary pneumothorax due to limited respiratory reserve. Management differs from primary pneumothorax: intercostal drain insertion is first-line rather than needle aspiration, as aspiration has a low success rate in diseased lungs. All patients with secondary pneumothorax should be admitted. Referral for surgical pleurodesis should be considered after first episode given the high recurrence rate (40-50%).
key_points: Intercostal drain is first-line for secondary pneumothorax (not needle aspiration)
Secondary pneumothorax is more dangerous than primary due to limited respiratory reserve
All secondary pneumothorax patients should be admitted to hospital
Small-bore drains (10-14F) are preferred over large-bore
Recurrence rate is 40-50% - early surgical referral for pleurodesis should be considered after first episode
explanation.pearls: Large emphysematous bullae on CT can mimic pneumothorax on plain X-ray in COPD patients - inserting a drain into a bulla is dangerous; if there is any diagnostic uncertainty, CT should be obtained before intervention.

options.rationale: Needle aspiration is first-line for primary spontaneous pneumothorax but is not recommended for secondary pneumothorax. The success rate of aspiration in secondary pneumothorax is significantly lower (approximately 30-40% vs 70-80% in primary) due to the underlying lung disease preventing re-expansion. Guidelines recommend intercostal drain as first-line for secondary pneumothorax. (Source: BTS: Pneumothorax Guidelines)

Observation may be considered for very small secondary pneumothorax (<1 cm) in minimally symptomatic patients, but this patient is significantly more symptomatic than baseline (SpO2 dropped from 91% to 85%, tachycardic, tachypnoeic). A moderate pneumothorax in severe COPD is poorly tolerated and requires active drainage. (Source: BTS: Pneumothorax Guidelines)

While supplemental oxygen assists pneumothorax reabsorption and treats hypoxia, high-flow oxygen alone does not address a moderate secondary pneumothorax in a patient with severe COPD. There is also a risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure with excessive oxygen in COPD patients. Active drainage is required alongside titrated oxygen therapy. (Source: BTS: Pneumothorax Guidelines)

CT can help differentiate pneumothorax from large bullae in COPD patients, which is an important distinction. However, in this case the diagnosis is clear on chest X-ray, and the patient is acutely deteriorating. Delaying drainage for CT imaging risks further deterioration. CT may be performed after initial stabilisation if there is diagnostic uncertainty. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in a patient with significant underlying lung disease requires intercostal drain insertion as first-line management. A small-bore catheter (10-14F) connected to an underwater seal drain is recommended. This patient has severe COPD with limited respiratory reserve, and the pneumothorax has caused significant desaturation below his baseline. Admission, drainage, and respiratory monitoring are essential. Suction may be added if the lung fails to re-expand. (Source: BTS: Pneumothorax Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Shingles in an adult under 50 who is not otherwise immunosuppressed is an HIV indicator condition. The National HIV Testing Policy lists conditions in which the undiagnosed HIV prevalence is high enough that a test should be offered routinely, and multidermatomal or severe zoster in a young adult is one of them. Testing needs consent and an explanation of how the result will be given, but no longer needs formal pre-test counselling in most settings. In context, late HIV diagnosis in Australia most often follows missed indicator conditions such as zoster, oral candidiasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, unexplained weight loss and recurrent bacterial pneumonia; offering a test whenever one appears is what moves diagnosis earlier.
key_points: Zoster under 50 without another cause of immunosuppression is an HIV indicator condition.
Consent is required, formal pre-test counselling generally is not.
Other indicator conditions include oral candidiasis, unexplained weight loss and seborrhoeic dermatitis.
A negative test in a man with ongoing risk is also the opening for a pre-exposure prophylaxis discussion.
explanation.pearls: Multidermatomal zoster, zoster that crosses the midline, and ophthalmic zoster in a young adult all warrant an HIV test even when the patient reports no risk exposure.

options.rationale: Herpes zoster in an adult under 50, particularly multidermatomal disease, is a recognised indicator condition and the National HIV Testing Policy directs that a test be offered whenever one is present. (Source: National HIV Testing Policy; RACGP Red Book)

Amitriptyline is for established postherpetic neuralgia that persists beyond rash healing, not prophylaxis at the crusting stage, and it addresses none of the reason this man developed zoster so young. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

Immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets belong in the work-up of recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infection or suspected primary immunodeficiency, and they would follow rather than replace an HIV test here. (Source: National HIV Testing Policy)

Imaging for occult malignancy is reasonable when zoster occurs with weight loss, lymphadenopathy or abnormal blood counts, none of which are present, and it is a far lower yield first test than serology. (Source: RACGP Red Book)

Recombinant zoster vaccine is given to prevent a first or recurrent episode, is deferred until the acute rash resolves, and is funded from age 65 or from 18 years in specified immunocompromising conditions. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: OI prophylaxis in HIV is guided by CD4 thresholds. PJP prophylaxis (TMP-SMX) at CD4 <200, toxoplasmosis prophylaxis at CD4 <100 if seropositive, and MAC prophylaxis at CD4 <50. TMP-SMX covers both PJP and toxoplasmosis. Prophylaxis continues until CD4 is sustained above the relevant threshold on ART, typically after 3-6 months.
key_points: PJP prophylaxis: CD4 <200 - TMP-SMX first-line
Toxoplasmosis prophylaxis: CD4 <100 + positive IgG - TMP-SMX double-strength
MAC prophylaxis: CD4 <50 - azithromycin
CMV: monitor with fundoscopy at CD4 <50, no universal prophylaxis
Cease prophylaxis when CD4 sustained above threshold for 3-6 months on ART
explanation.pearls: TMP-SMX double-strength daily simultaneously covers PJP prophylaxis (CD4 <200) and toxoplasmosis prophylaxis (CD4 <100 with positive IgG) - the dose for dual coverage is 160/800 mg daily, compared to 80/400 mg or thrice-weekly for PJP-only prophylaxis.

options.rationale: CMV prophylaxis with valganciclovir is not recommended for primary prophylaxis in HIV. CMV disease prophylaxis is considered only at CD4 <50, and even then, universal prophylaxis is not standard practice - regular fundoscopy for CMV retinitis is preferred. CMV IgG positivity indicates past exposure, not active disease. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

MAC prophylaxis with azithromycin is indicated at CD4 <50. Her CD4 is 85, above this threshold. Adding azithromycin would be unnecessary medication with potential side effects and drug interactions. TMP-SMX alone covers the relevant pathogens at her CD4 level. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

While ART will restore immune function, the time to CD4 recovery above prophylaxis thresholds is typically 3-6 months. During this vulnerable period, the patient remains at risk. Prophylaxis bridges the gap until immune reconstitution occurs. It can be ceased once CD4 is sustained above threshold on ART. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

Dapsone plus pyrimethamine is an alternative for patients intolerant of TMP-SMX. TMP-SMX is first-line due to superior efficacy, dual PJP/toxoplasmosis coverage in a single agent, and additional benefit against some bacterial infections. Dapsone is reserved for sulfonamide allergy. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

At CD4 <200, PJP prophylaxis with TMP-SMX is indicated. At CD4 <100 with positive Toxoplasma IgG, toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is also indicated - TMP-SMX at double-strength daily dose covers both. Her CD4 of 85 triggers both thresholds. MAC prophylaxis is not needed as CD4 is above 50. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: IRIS occurs when recovering immune function on ART generates an exaggerated inflammatory response against previously subclinical or treated opportunistic infections. TB-IRIS is the most common form, presenting as new or worsening lymphadenopathy, consolidation, or effusions despite virological response to ART. It typically occurs 1-8 weeks after ART initiation, particularly when baseline CD4 is very low.
key_points: IRIS occurs with IMPROVING immunological parameters (rising CD4, falling VL)
TB-IRIS is the most common form - new symptoms despite ART response
Risk factors: very low baseline CD4, high VL, starting ART close to OI treatment
Management: continue ART, treat TB, add corticosteroids if severe
Distinguish from ART failure (rising VL) and drug resistance
explanation.pearls: TB-IRIS risk is highest when ART is commenced within 2 weeks of TB treatment initiation and baseline CD4 is below 50 - the PredART trial showed that prednisone 40 mg daily for 2 weeks then 20 mg for 2 weeks reduces TB-IRIS incidence by 30% in high-risk patients.

options.rationale: ART treatment failure would show RISING viral load and FALLING CD4. This patient shows the opposite: VL has dropped from 320,000 to 2,500 and CD4 has risen from 45 to 120. This pattern confirms virological response to ART, not failure. The worsening clinical picture paradoxically accompanies immunological improvement. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

This is classic unmasking TB-IRIS. He was treated for latent TB but may have had undiagnosed subclinical active TB. As ART restored immune function (CD4 rise, VL drop), the recovering immune system mounted an inflammatory response against previously subclinical mycobacterial disease. New lymphadenopathy and consolidation in the context of rising CD4 on ART is the hallmark presentation. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

While CAP is possible, the combination of new lymphadenopathy, consolidation, and clinical deterioration in the context of recent ART initiation with rising CD4 strongly suggests IRIS rather than a new community-acquired infection. The fluctuant lymphadenopathy is particularly suggestive of mycobacterial IRIS. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

While drug-resistant TB should be considered, the timing (3 weeks after ART with improving viral/immunological parameters) points to IRIS as the mechanism. Drug resistance would be expected to present independently of immune reconstitution. Drug susceptibility testing should be performed on any cultured organisms but IRIS remains the most likely explanation. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

ART hypersensitivity (particularly abacavir) can cause fever and systemic symptoms, but new focal consolidation and fluctuant lymphadenopathy are not typical drug reaction features. The pattern is organ-specific (lung and nodes) consistent with IRIS against a mycobacterial antigen. (Source: AMH; ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: In patients with chronic hepatitis B starting tenofovir-containing PrEP, the critical concern is HBV flare on cessation. Tenofovir-emtricitabine suppresses HBV replication. If PrEP is discontinued, viral rebound can trigger severe hepatitis flare potentially leading to hepatic decompensation. This does not preclude PrEP but requires hepatology involvement, informed consent, and a HBV management plan for any future PrEP cessation.
key_points: Tenofovir-emtricitabine PrEP treats HBV concurrently - this is beneficial
HBV flare risk on PrEP cessation is the critical concern
Hepatology review recommended before starting - not a contraindication
Daily PrEP preferred over on-demand in HBV co-infection
Monitor HBV DNA and LFTs during and after any PrEP changes
explanation.pearls: Tenofovir-emtricitabine PrEP cessation in HBsAg-positive patients can trigger HBV flares within 2-8 weeks, with ALT elevations up to 10x ULN reported - all PrEP prescribers must check HBsAg before initiation and involve hepatology if positive.

options.rationale: While STI screening is part of routine PrEP assessment, treated gonorrhoea 6 weeks ago does not require test-of-cure before PrEP initiation. Current STI screen is negative. PrEP should not be delayed for this reason when the patient is at ongoing high risk. (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines)

Active HBV is not an absolute contraindication to PrEP. Tenofovir-emtricitabine provides dual benefit (HIV prevention and HBV treatment). The critical issue is management of cessation risk, not prohibition. Denying PrEP to a high-risk individual due to a manageable concern is not best practice. (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines)

eGFR 92 is well above the standard PrEP threshold. Tenofovir disoproxil PrEP is generally safe with eGFR above 60 (some guidelines use >50). eGFR monitoring every 3-6 months is recommended during PrEP but initiation at eGFR 92 is appropriate. (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines; AMH)

Tenofovir disoproxil-emtricitabine (the standard PrEP regimen) is also active against HBV. In a patient with chronic active hepatitis B (HBeAg+, high viral load), commencing and then discontinuing PrEP could trigger a severe hepatitis B flare from loss of antiviral suppression. He needs gastroenterology/hepatology review to: (1) assess if HBV treatment is independently indicated, (2) counsel about flare risk on PrEP cessation, (3) establish monitoring. PrEP can proceed but with informed consent about this risk and a plan for HBV management if PrEP is ever stopped. (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: GI)

On-demand PrEP is an option for MSM, but in this case with active HBV, daily dosing is actually preferred as it provides continuous HBV suppression. Event-driven dosing would create intermittent HBV suppression/rebound cycles, potentially worsening hepatic outcomes. Daily tenofovir-emtricitabine serves dual HIV prevention and HBV treatment purposes. (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: GI)

explanation.summary: HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis requires a structured treatment approach: induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine for 2 weeks, consolidation with fluconazole for 8 weeks, then long-term maintenance. Raised ICP is managed with daily therapeutic LPs, not steroids or mannitol. ART initiation must be DELAYED 4-6 weeks to reduce IRIS-related mortality. The COAT trial demonstrated increased mortality with early ART in cryptococcal meningitis.
key_points: Induction: amphotericin B + flucytosine for 2 weeks minimum
Daily therapeutic LPs for opening pressure >25 cmH2O
Corticosteroids are contraindicated in cryptococcal meningitis
DELAY ART for 4-6 weeks to reduce IRIS mortality
Consolidation: fluconazole 400 mg for 8 weeks, then maintenance 200 mg
explanation.pearls: The COAT trial (NEJM 2014) randomised cryptococcal meningitis patients to early ART (1-2 weeks) versus delayed ART (5 weeks) - early ART increased mortality by 15% absolute, establishing the standard of delaying ART 4-6 weeks until CSF sterilisation is confirmed.

options.rationale: Voriconazole is not recommended for cryptococcal meningitis. While it has antifungal activity, it is less effective than amphotericin B plus flucytosine for this indication. Voriconazole is primarily used for aspergillosis. The established induction regimen (amphotericin + flucytosine) has the strongest evidence base. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ASHM)

Fluconazole monotherapy, even at high dose, is inferior to amphotericin B plus flucytosine for induction and is associated with higher mortality. Mannitol does not effectively manage cryptococcal ICP - therapeutic LPs are the evidence-based approach as the ICP is caused by impaired CSF reabsorption, not cerebral oedema. (Source: ASHM; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Immediate ART initiation in cryptococcal meningitis increases mortality through IRIS. The COAT trial demonstrated that early ART (within 1-2 weeks) versus delayed ART (5 weeks) significantly increased mortality. ART should be delayed 4-6 weeks until CSF is sterilised and clinical stability is achieved. (Source: ASHM; COAT trial; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Corticosteroids are CONTRAINDICATED in HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. The evidence shows no benefit and potential harm from adjunctive dexamethasone (unlike bacterial meningitis where dexamethasone is beneficial). ICP management is through therapeutic LPs, not steroids. (Source: ASHM; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Cryptococcal meningitis management follows a structured protocol: 2-week induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, followed by consolidation with fluconazole 400 mg daily for 8 weeks, then maintenance fluconazole 200 mg daily. Raised intracranial pressure (>25 cmH2O) requires daily therapeutic LPs to reduce pressure by draining CSF until opening pressure is consistently below 20 cmH2O. ART should be DELAYED 4-6 weeks to reduce IRIS risk. (Source: ASHM; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: LTBI screening with IGRA (QuantiFERON) is preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals as it avoids BCG-related false positives.
