Positive IGRA with normal CXR and no symptoms indicates LTBI requiring treatment. Standard regimens include isoniazid for 9 months or rifampicin for 4 months. Refugees from high-burden countries are a priority population for LTBI treatment.
key_points: IGRA is preferred over TST in BCG-vaccinated individuals
QuantiFERON uses ESAT-6/CFP-10 antigens not present in BCG
LTBI: positive IGRA + normal CXR + no symptoms
Treatment: isoniazid 9 months or rifampicin 4 months
Pyridoxine 25 mg daily prevents isoniazid neuropathy
explanation.pearls: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus measures IFN-gamma responses to ESAT-6 and CFP-10 antigens which are absent from all BCG strains and most non-tuberculous mycobacteria - this gives it >95% specificity in BCG-vaccinated populations compared to 56-60% for TST.

options.rationale: Positive QuantiFERON in an asymptomatic patient with normal CXR indicates latent TB infection (LTBI). IGRA (QuantiFERON) is preferred over TST in BCG-vaccinated individuals as it is not affected by prior BCG. Treatment of LTBI is indicated in this high-risk patient (refugee from high-burden country). Standard regimens include isoniazid for 9 months or rifampicin for 4 months. Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; NTAC Guidelines)

QuantiFERON (IGRA) uses antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10) not present in BCG. Therefore, BCG vaccination does NOT cause false-positive IGRA results. A positive QuantiFERON in a BCG-vaccinated person indicates true M. tuberculosis infection. This is precisely why IGRA is preferred over TST in BCG-vaccinated populations. (Source: NTAC Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Positive IGRA with normal CXR and no symptoms indicates LTBI, not active TB. Full RIPE therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) is for active TB only. Over-treating LTBI with 4-drug therapy exposes the patient to unnecessary drug toxicity. Active TB requires clinical features or radiological/microbiological evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; NTAC Guidelines)

Sputum sampling for active TB is indicated when there are symptoms or abnormal CXR suggesting active disease. In an asymptomatic patient with normal CXR, sputum sampling is not indicated. The diagnosis of LTBI is based on positive IGRA with exclusion of active disease clinically and radiologically. (Source: NTAC Guidelines)

LTBI reactivation risk is lifelong and estimated at 5-10% overall, with highest risk in the first 2 years after infection and in immunosuppressive states. Refugees from high-burden countries are a priority group for LTBI treatment. Delaying treatment without indication is not recommended when the patient is eligible and willing. (Source: NTAC Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Smear-positive pulmonary TB requires immediate notification to the public health unit, respiratory isolation in a negative-pressure room, and contact tracing. TB is notifiable in all Australian jurisdictions. Cavitary smear-positive disease is highly infectious. Contact tracing begins immediately and does not wait for culture or susceptibility results. The public health unit coordinates the response.
key_points: TB is notifiable to state public health unit within 24 hours of suspicion
Smear-positive cavitary TB requires negative-pressure isolation
Contact tracing begins immediately, not after culture/DST
Non-infectiousness: typically after 2 weeks treatment + clinical improvement + negative smears
Notification obligation is on treating doctor AND laboratory independently
explanation.pearls: Smear-positive cavitary TB has a bacterial load of 10^7-10^9 organisms per mL of sputum compared to 10^3-10^5 in smear-negative disease - cavitary patients are 5-10x more infectious and require strict respiratory isolation until rendered non-infectious.

options.rationale: While AFB smear detects acid-fast bacilli (which include NTM), in the clinical context of cavitary disease with compatible symptoms, smear-positive disease is treated as TB until proven otherwise. Notification should not be delayed for culture (which takes 2-8 weeks). Public health units are notified on clinical suspicion with smear positivity. (Source: NTAC Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Smear-positive cavitary TB requires hospital-based respiratory isolation until he is rendered non-infectious (typically after 2 weeks of effective treatment with clinical improvement and three negative sputum smears). A taxi driver with cavitary TB poses a public health risk. Home isolation is insufficient for smear-positive disease with high bacillary load. (Source: NTAC Guidelines; NSW Health TB Protocol)

TB is a notifiable disease in all Australian states and territories. Smear-positive cavitary TB is highly infectious. Immediate actions include: respiratory isolation (negative-pressure room with N95 masks for staff), notification to public health unit within 24 hours, and initiation of contact tracing including close household and occupational contacts (taxi passengers are generally not traced unless prolonged exposure). (Source: NTAC Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; NSW Health TB Protocol)

Contact tracing should commence immediately, not wait for DST (which takes 4-8 weeks for culture-based methods). Contacts need screening regardless of drug susceptibility. DST results may later inform treatment decisions for the index case but do not affect the urgency of identifying exposed contacts. (Source: NTAC Guidelines)

TB notification goes to the state/territory public health unit, not just the GP. In most jurisdictions, both the treating doctor and the laboratory have independent notification obligations. The public health unit coordinates contact tracing, directly observed therapy, and ensures treatment completion. (Source: NTAC Guidelines; NSW Health TB Protocol)

explanation.summary: Anti-TB drug hepatotoxicity occurs in 5-10% of patients on RIPE therapy. ALT >5x ULN (or >3x with symptoms) mandates cessation of hepatotoxic agents. The standard approach is to cease isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide, continue ethambutol (non-hepatotoxic), and sequentially reintroduce once LFTs normalise. Rifampicin is typically reintroduced first, then isoniazid, then pyrazinamide last.
key_points: Cease hepatotoxic agents if ALT >5x ULN or >3x with symptoms
Pyrazinamide > isoniazid > rifampicin in hepatotoxicity risk
Ethambutol is not hepatotoxic and can continue
Sequential reintroduction: rifampicin first, then isoniazid, then pyrazinamide
If pyrazinamide cannot be reintroduced, extend total treatment to 9 months
explanation.pearls: When pyrazinamide is permanently omitted due to hepatotoxicity, the intensive phase shortens to 2 months of rifampicin plus isoniazid plus ethambutol, but the total treatment duration extends from 6 to 9 months to compensate for the lost sterilising activity of pyrazinamide.

options.rationale: Dose reduction does not adequately address drug-induced hepatotoxicity at this severity (ALT 17x ULN with symptoms). The standard approach is cessation of hepatotoxic agents, not dose reduction. Sub-therapeutic dosing also risks drug resistance development. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; NTAC Guidelines)

ALT >5x ULN with symptoms constitutes drug-induced hepatotoxicity requiring cessation of all potentially hepatotoxic agents. Pyrazinamide is the most hepatotoxic, followed by isoniazid, then rifampicin. Ethambutol is not hepatotoxic and can continue. Sequential reintroduction after LFT normalisation (typically rifampicin first, then isoniazid, then pyrazinamide last or omitted) allows identification of the causative agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; NTAC Guidelines)

While pyrazinamide is the most hepatotoxic, with ALT 17x ULN, all potentially hepatotoxic agents should be ceased. Continuing isoniazid and rifampicin with this degree of hepatotoxicity risks progression to fulminant liver failure. Sequential reintroduction identifies the specific causative agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Mild asymptomatic transaminase elevation (ALT <3x ULN) can be monitored without cessation. However, ALT 380 (17x ULN) with symptoms (nausea, vomiting, RUQ pain) exceeds all thresholds for continued treatment. This is significant hepatotoxicity requiring drug cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; NTAC Guidelines)

A permanent switch to second-line agents is premature before attempting sequential reintroduction. Many patients can tolerate reintroduced rifampicin and isoniazid - pyrazinamide is most commonly the culprit and can be omitted (extending treatment to 9 months). Second-line regimens are reserved for patients who cannot tolerate any first-line hepatotoxic agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; NTAC Guidelines)

explanation.summary: GeneXpert rifampicin resistance in a patient with previous incomplete TB treatment strongly indicates MDR-TB. Management requires specialist TB service involvement, empiric MDR-TB regimen (not standard RIPE), directly observed therapy, and isolation. Modern shorter MDR-TB regimens (BPaL - bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid) have improved outcomes. Full DST guides regimen refinement but should not delay empiric treatment.
key_points: GeneXpert rifampicin resistance = MDR-TB until proven otherwise
Incomplete previous treatment is the strongest risk factor for drug resistance
MDR-TB treatment requires specialist TB service and DOT
Do not wait for full DST - start empiric MDR regimen immediately
PNG is a high MDR-TB burden country bordering Australia
explanation.pearls: The BPaL regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid) for MDR-TB has achieved cure rates exceeding 90% in the TB-PRACTECAL trial with only 6 months of treatment - a paradigm shift from the previous 18-24 month injectable-based regimens with 50-60% cure rates.

options.rationale: Simply adding moxifloxacin to RIPE is not adequate MDR-TB treatment. If rifampicin is resistant, the rifampicin component is ineffective. If isoniazid is also resistant (likely in MDR-TB), the regimen collapses to pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and moxifloxacin - suboptimal. MDR-TB requires specifically designed regimens under specialist guidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; WHO MDR-TB Guidelines)

GeneXpert has >95% sensitivity and >98% specificity for rifampicin resistance. In a patient with previous incomplete treatment from a high MDR-TB burden country (PNG), the pre-test probability is very high making a false positive extremely unlikely. Starting standard RIPE with rifampicin-resistant TB would be ineffective, risking further resistance development and clinical deterioration. (Source: NTAC Guidelines)

GeneXpert rifampicin resistance in a patient with previous incomplete treatment strongly suggests MDR-TB (resistance to at least rifampicin and isoniazid). This requires specialist infectious diseases/respiratory physician management at a designated TB service. Treatment is complex (typically 9-20 month regimen with fluoroquinolone, bedaquiline, linezolid, and other agents), requires directly observed therapy (DOT), and close monitoring. Culture and full DST must be sent but should not delay empiric MDR treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; NTAC MDR-TB Guidelines)

Phenotypic DST takes 4-8 weeks from culture. Waiting this long before treating smear-positive TB with rifampicin resistance risks clinical deterioration and ongoing transmission. Empiric MDR-TB treatment should begin immediately based on GeneXpert results while awaiting full DST to refine the regimen. (Source: NTAC Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

While non-adherence caused the initial treatment failure, incomplete treatment is the primary driver of acquired drug resistance. GeneXpert has confirmed rifampicin resistance. Re-treating with RIPE would be ineffective against resistant organisms and would risk amplifying resistance to remaining drugs. (Source: NTAC Guidelines; WHO MDR-TB Guidelines)

explanation.summary: In TB-HIV co-infection with CD4 <50, ART should begin within 2 weeks of TB treatment. This is based on landmark trials (SAPIT, CAMELIA, STRIDE) showing mortality reduction despite increased IRIS risk. The exception is TB meningitis where early ART increases mortality. Drug interactions (rifampicin with ARTs) are manageable - dolutegravir dose is doubled to 50 mg BD with rifampicin.
key_points: CD4 <50: ART within 2 weeks of TB treatment start
CD4 >50: ART can be deferred to 8 weeks after TB treatment
Exception: TB meningitis - delay ART 4-8 weeks
Rifampicin + dolutegravir: increase dolutegravir to 50 mg BD
IRIS is managed if it occurs, not avoided by delaying ART
explanation.pearls: The SAPIT trial showed that among TB-HIV patients with CD4 <50, early ART (within 4 weeks of TB treatment) reduced mortality by 56% compared to delayed ART (after intensive phase) - the NNT to prevent one death was 6, establishing early ART as one of the highest-impact interventions in HIV medicine.

options.rationale: Multiple RCTs (SAPIT, CAMELIA, STRIDE) demonstrate that early ART (within 2 weeks of TB treatment) reduces mortality in patients with CD4 <50 compared to delayed ART (8-12 weeks). The mortality benefit outweighs the IRIS risk at this level of immunosuppression. IRIS is managed if it occurs rather than avoided by delaying essential treatment. The exception is TB meningitis and cryptococcal meningitis where ART is delayed. (Source: ASHM; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; SAPIT trial)

Waiting 2 months in a patient with CD4 38 increases mortality. While drug interactions exist (particularly rifampicin with protease inhibitors and some integrase inhibitors), these are manageable. Dolutegravir at doubled dose (50 mg BD instead of daily) or efavirenz at standard dose can be used with rifampicin. (Source: ASHM; SAPIT trial)

Delayed ART for IRIS prevention was studied in the SAPIT and CAMELIA trials and found to increase mortality at CD4 <50. The mortality reduction from early ART exceeds the morbidity from IRIS. Delayed ART is only appropriate when CD4 is >50, or in TB meningitis or concurrent cryptococcal meningitis. (Source: ASHM; CAMELIA trial)

Same-day initiation of ART and TB treatment is not recommended. Starting both simultaneously makes it difficult to distinguish drug side effects and intolerances between the two regimens. The standard recommendation for CD4 <50 is within 2 weeks (not day 1) of TB treatment to allow initial TB drug tolerance assessment. (Source: ASHM; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Waiting for DST (4-8 weeks) delays ART by an unacceptable duration in a patient with CD4 38. ART should be started within 2 weeks regardless of pending DST. If DST later reveals resistance, the TB regimen is modified, but this does not affect ART timing. (Source: ASHM; NTAC Guidelines)

explanation.summary: This patient presents with sepsis secondary to a urinary tract source, meeting qSOFA criteria (altered mental status, systolic BP less than 100 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 or more). The hour-1 sepsis bundle requires blood cultures before antibiotics, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension, and lactate measurement. For severe urosepsis, eTG Antibiotic recommends gentamicin plus ampicillin to cover gram-negative organisms and enterococci. The elevated lactate of 4.2 mmol/L indicates tissue hypoperfusion and should prompt aggressive resuscitation.
key_points: qSOFA score of 3 (confusion, hypotension, tachypnoea) identifies high-risk sepsis requiring urgent intervention
Hour-1 bundle: blood cultures before antibiotics, empiric antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, lactate measurement
Gentamicin plus ampicillin is the recommended empiric regimen for severe urosepsis per eTG Antibiotic
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin dosing in sepsis is 5 mg/kg IV (ideal body weight) with monitoring of renal function and drug levels. Lactate greater than 4 mmol/L is associated with significantly increased mortality and mandates aggressive resuscitation within 1 hour.

options.rationale: This patient has sepsis secondary to a urinary source with haemodynamic compromise. The eTG Antibiotic recommends gentamicin plus ampicillin as empiric therapy for severe urosepsis, providing gram-negative and enterococcal coverage. Blood cultures must be obtained before antibiotic administration, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid should be commenced for hypotension as part of the hour-1 bundle. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

This combination is more appropriate for intra-abdominal sepsis rather than urosepsis. Metronidazole provides anaerobic coverage that is not required for a urinary tract source. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Piperacillin-tazobactam provides broad-spectrum coverage but is not recommended as first-line empiric therapy for urosepsis in Australian guidelines. It may be considered in specific situations such as known resistant organisms or healthcare-associated infections. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Amoxicillin-clavulanate may be used for less severe urinary infections but provides insufficient coverage for severe urosepsis with septic shock physiology. It lacks reliable activity against many gram-negative organisms causing complicated UTIs. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Fluoroquinolones are not first-line for urosepsis in Australian guidelines due to resistance concerns and adverse effects. Vancomycin adds unnecessary MRSA coverage when there is no clinical indication for it in this presentation. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: This patient has fluid-refractory septic shock with persistent hypotension (MAP 58 mmHg), rising lactate, metabolic acidosis, oliguria, and worsening oxygenation despite 30 mL/kg crystalloid. The next step is initiation of noradrenaline as the first-line vasopressor, targeting a MAP of 65 mmHg or greater. Noradrenaline can be commenced via a peripheral intravenous line while central access is established. Hydrocortisone at 200 mg/day should be considered if the patient remains vasopressor-dependent despite adequate doses. ICU referral should occur early in the resuscitation process.
key_points: Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor for fluid-refractory septic shock with a MAP target of 65 mmHg or greater
Vasopressors should not be delayed for central venous access - peripheral administration is acceptable as a bridge
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day is reserved for vasopressor-refractory shock, not as a first-line haemodynamic agent
explanation.pearls: Noradrenaline can be safely administered via a peripheral IV cannula at concentrations up to 8 mcg/mL for initial resuscitation. Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV 6-hourly (total 200 mg/day) should be considered when noradrenaline requirements exceed 0.25 mcg/kg/min.

options.rationale: The patient has already received the recommended initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation and remains hypotensive with a rising lactate. Further large-volume fluid boluses without vasopressor support risk fluid overload and worsening pulmonary oedema, particularly in the context of her declining oxygenation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor for septic shock refractory to initial crystalloid resuscitation. It should be commenced when hypotension persists despite 30 mL/kg fluid resuscitation, targeting a MAP of 65 mmHg or greater. It can be started via peripheral IV while central venous access is being arranged. The rising lactate and metabolic acidosis indicate worsening tissue hypoperfusion requiring urgent haemodynamic support. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Adrenaline is not the recommended first-line vasopressor in septic shock. While it provides both vasopressor and inotropic effects, it is associated with greater tachycardia and metabolic side effects including lactic acidosis, which complicates lactate monitoring. It may be considered as a second-line agent or when additional inotropic support is needed. (Source: ANZICS)

Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg 6-hourly) is recommended for septic shock that remains refractory despite adequate fluid resuscitation and vasopressor therapy. It should not be commenced before a vasopressor trial, as it is an adjunctive measure for vasopressor-refractory shock rather than a first-line haemodynamic agent. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Vasopressin is a second-line vasopressor in septic shock. It may be added to noradrenaline to reduce catecholamine requirements or as an alternative if arrhythmias develop, but it is not recommended as the initial vasopressor ahead of noradrenaline per current guidelines. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: This young immunocompetent woman presents with classic features of bacterial meningitis. She has no indications for CT before LP (GCS 15, no focal deficits, not immunocompromised, no seizures). The priority is dexamethasone 10 mg IV given before or with the first antibiotic dose, followed by ceftriaxone 2 g IV BD. Dexamethasone should be continued at 10 mg IV 6-hourly for 4 days if pneumococcal meningitis is confirmed. Lumbar puncture should be performed promptly but must not delay antibiotic administration.
key_points: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV must be given before or with the first dose of antibiotics to reduce mortality and neurological sequelae
CT before LP is only indicated for focal neurology, GCS less than 12, immunocompromise, or new seizures
Empiric ceftriaxone 2 g IV BD is standard for immunocompetent adults aged 18 to 50 with suspected bacterial meningitis
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly for 4 days should be continued if Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified but can be ceased if an alternative organism is confirmed. Listeria coverage with benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is added for patients over 50 years, pregnant, or immunocompromised.

options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics until imaging and CSF results are available is inappropriate in suspected bacterial meningitis. In this patient with no indications for CT before LP (no focal deficits, GCS 15, immunocompetent, no new seizures), antibiotics should be given as soon as possible. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

While LP can proceed without CT in this patient, waiting for CSF confirmation before commencing antibiotics is inappropriate. Empiric antibiotics should be administered as soon as possible - ideally within 60 minutes of presentation. Delays in antibiotic administration are associated with increased mortality. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

In suspected bacterial meningitis with no contraindications to LP, dexamethasone 10 mg IV should be given before or with the first dose of antibiotics, followed by ceftriaxone 2 g IV BD. Dexamethasone reduces mortality and neurological sequelae, particularly in pneumococcal meningitis. This patient has no indications for CT before LP (GCS 15, no focal deficits, immunocompetent, no new seizures), so LP can proceed after treatment is initiated. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Adding benzylpenicillin to ceftriaxone is unnecessary in a young immunocompetent patient. Benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is added for Listeria coverage in patients older than 50, immunocompromised, or pregnant. Omitting dexamethasone is also incorrect, as adjunctive dexamethasone is recommended in suspected bacterial meningitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

CT before LP is indicated when there are focal neurological deficits, GCS less than 12, immunocompromise, or new-onset seizures. This patient has none of these features, so CT is not required before LP. Importantly, even when CT is indicated, antibiotics should not be delayed pending imaging. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: This patient presents with the classic triad of HSV encephalitis: fever, altered behaviour or personality change, and seizures with temporal lobe predilection. The CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein and relatively preserved glucose, consistent with a viral aetiology. IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly must be started empirically as soon as HSV encephalitis is suspected, as delays in treatment significantly worsen outcomes. MRI brain typically shows temporal lobe signal abnormality on T2/FLAIR sequences. CSF HSV PCR is the gold standard diagnostic test but must not delay empiric treatment.
key_points: HSV encephalitis classically presents with fever, personality change, temporal lobe seizures, and confusion
IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly must be commenced empirically and not delayed for investigations
CSF in viral encephalitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and preserved or mildly low glucose
explanation.pearls: Aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly is continued for 14 to 21 days for confirmed HSV encephalitis. Adequate IV hydration is essential to prevent aciclovir-induced crystalline nephropathy. CSF HSV PCR may be negative in the first 72 hours and should be repeated if clinical suspicion remains high.

options.rationale: While ceftriaxone covers bacterial meningitis, the CSF profile here shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein and relatively preserved glucose, which is characteristic of viral rather than bacterial aetiology. The clinical presentation with behavioural change, seizures, and fever strongly suggests HSV encephalitis, which requires IV aciclovir. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

While MRI is important for diagnosis (temporal lobe signal abnormality supports HSV encephalitis), treatment must not be delayed pending imaging. IV aciclovir should be commenced empirically as soon as HSV encephalitis is suspected, given the significant morbidity and mortality associated with treatment delays. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

CSF HSV PCR is the confirmatory test but results are not available immediately. Delaying aciclovir for PCR confirmation is inappropriate because untreated HSV encephalitis has mortality exceeding 70%. Empiric aciclovir must be commenced on clinical suspicion alone. A negative early PCR does not exclude HSV encephalitis and may need repeating. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

This presentation of fever, behavioural change, seizures, and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein and preserved glucose is highly suspicious for HSV encephalitis. Aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly must be commenced empirically without delay. MRI brain will typically show temporal lobe signal abnormality and should be arranged but must not delay treatment. CSF HSV PCR should be sent for confirmation. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Oral valaciclovir is not appropriate for the treatment of HSV encephalitis. Intravenous aciclovir at 10 mg/kg 8-hourly is required to achieve adequate CNS drug concentrations. Oral valaciclovir is used for less severe herpes simplex infections such as genital herpes or herpes zoster. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Migraine prevention should be considered when attacks occur 4 or more days per month, when acute treatments are ineffective, or when there is significant disability. First-line preventive agents in Australia include propranolol, amitriptyline, and candesartan. This patient has asthma, which contraindicates propranolol, and is taking the combined oral contraceptive pill, which interacts with topiramate. Amitriptyline is appropriate as it avoids both these issues. Notably, this patient also has migraine with aura, which is itself a reason to reconsider the combined oral contraceptive pill due to increased stroke risk.
key_points: Migraine prevention is indicated when attacks occur 4 or more days per month or cause significant disability
Beta-blockers are contraindicated in patients with asthma due to risk of bronchospasm
Triptans are acute treatments only and should not be used for migraine prevention
explanation.pearls: Amitriptyline for migraine prevention is started at 10 mg at night and titrated to a typical dose of 25 to 50 mg over several weeks. A preventive trial should be continued for at least 2 to 3 months at adequate dose before assessing efficacy. Migraine with aura combined with the oral contraceptive pill increases ischaemic stroke risk.

options.rationale: Propranolol is a first-line migraine preventive agent, but it is contraindicated in this patient due to her history of asthma. Beta-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm and should be avoided in patients with asthma. (Source: eTG Neurology)

Triptans are acute migraine treatments and are not indicated for prevention. Daily triptan use risks medication overuse headache when used more than 10 days per month. Triptans should be reserved for acute episodic treatment. (Source: Headache Australia)

Topiramate is an effective migraine preventive agent but requires specific counselling regarding teratogenicity. It interacts with the combined oral contraceptive pill by reducing its efficacy through hepatic enzyme induction. While it could be considered, the interaction with her current contraception and the availability of safer alternatives make it less appropriate as first choice. (Source: AMH)

Verapamil is the first-line preventive agent for cluster headache, not migraine. It is not recommended as a standard preventive therapy for migraine in Australian guidelines. Appropriate first-line migraine preventive agents include propranolol, amitriptyline, and candesartan. (Source: eTG Neurology)

Amitriptyline is a first-line migraine preventive agent that is appropriate for this patient. It avoids the beta-blocker contraindication due to asthma and the drug interaction concerns with topiramate and the oral contraceptive pill. It is started at a low dose of 10 mg at night and titrated upwards. Common side effects include drowsiness and dry mouth. (Source: eTG Neurology)

explanation.summary: Cluster headache management has three arms. Abortive treatment, oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan, works on the individual attack. Preventive treatment, verapamil first-line, takes one to two weeks to reach an effective dose. Transitional treatment bridges that gap: a short high-dose oral corticosteroid course, commonly prednisolone 50 mg daily for about five days followed by a taper, suppresses attacks within a day or two and is stopped once the preventer is working, since repeated or prolonged courses risk avascular necrosis and the other steroid harms. A greater occipital nerve block is the alternative bridge where available. In context: patients in a bout can have several attacks daily, and recognising that the fast abortive, the slow preventer and the bridge are three separate decisions is the exam point.
key_points: Transitional therapy bridges the one to two weeks while verapamil is titrated
Prednisolone about 50 mg daily for five days then taper, not a prolonged course
Greater occipital nerve block is the alternative bridge
Subcutaneous sumatriptan is capped at two doses in 24 hours
explanation.pearls: If attacks return every time the steroid is withdrawn, the preventer dose is inadequate rather than the bridge being too short.

options.rationale: A short oral corticosteroid course is standard transitional therapy, suppressing attacks within a day or two while verapamil is titrated to an effective dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Two subcutaneous doses in 24 hours is the limit; exceeding it is not appropriate, and frequent attacks are a reason to add transitional and preventive cover. (Source: AMH: Sumatriptan)

Lithium is a later-line preventer in chronic cluster headache when verapamil has failed or is not tolerated, under specialist supervision with level monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Amitriptyline helps chronic tension-type headache and migraine prevention, especially with disturbed sleep. It has no role in cluster headache. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Parenteral opioid is for severe pain without a faster specific treatment. Attacks resolve before it works, and repeated use in a relapsing condition causes harm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension predominantly affects young women with obesity and is characterised by raised intracranial pressure without a structural cause. Diagnosis requires papilloedema, elevated LP opening pressure (greater than 25 cmH2O in adults), normal CSF composition, and exclusion of secondary causes including cerebral venous sinus thrombosis on MR venography. Key symptoms include progressive headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, and visual field deficits. The combined oral contraceptive pill is a recognised exacerbating factor and should be ceased. Management centres on acetazolamide, weight loss, and regular visual monitoring.
key_points: Diagnosis requires papilloedema, LP opening pressure greater than 25 cmH2O, normal CSF composition, and exclusion of venous sinus thrombosis
Acetazolamide 250 mg BD titrated to response is first-line pharmacotherapy, with sustained weight loss of 5 to 10% for long-term remission
Surgical intervention (optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting) is reserved for rapidly progressive visual loss refractory to medical therapy
explanation.pearls: Acetazolamide is started at 250 mg BD and can be titrated to a maximum of 4 g/day. Patients should be warned about paraesthesiae, dysgeusia, and the risk of renal calculi. MR venography is essential to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which mimics idiopathic intracranial hypertension but requires anticoagulation.

options.rationale: While topiramate has weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor activity and may promote weight loss, it is not the first-line pharmacological treatment for idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Acetazolamide is the established first-line agent with better evidence for reducing CSF pressure and improving visual outcomes. Topiramate may be considered if acetazolamide is not tolerated. (Source: eTG Neurology)

Optic nerve sheath fenestration is reserved for rapidly progressive or severe visual loss that is not responding to medical therapy, or as a temporising measure in fulminant disease. This patient has mildly reduced acuity and enlarged blind spots without evidence of rapidly progressive visual loss, so surgical intervention is not indicated initially. Medical management should be trialled first. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

This patient meets diagnostic criteria for idiopathic intracranial hypertension: papilloedema, elevated opening pressure (greater than 25 cmH2O), normal CSF composition, normal MRI with no venous sinus thrombosis, and no alternative diagnosis. Initial management includes acetazolamide 250 mg BD (titrated up as needed to a maximum of 4 g/day), cessation of the combined oral contraceptive pill which may exacerbate the condition, and sustained weight loss of 5 to 10% which is the only intervention shown to achieve long-term remission. Regular ophthalmological review is essential. (Source: eTG Neurology)

Furosemide is not first-line therapy for idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Serial therapeutic lumbar punctures provide only transient relief and are not a sustainable management strategy. CSF is regenerated within hours, so the benefit is short-lived. Acetazolamide is the first-line pharmacological agent. (Source: eTG Neurology)

Corticosteroids may provide short-term reduction in intracranial pressure but are not appropriate for ongoing management of idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Chronic corticosteroid use exacerbates weight gain and can paradoxically worsen the condition on withdrawal. They may be considered as a very short-term bridge in fulminant disease. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: This young man presents with acute myocarditis following a viral prodrome. Key discriminators from pericarditis include significant troponin elevation, reduced LVEF with global hypokinesis, elevated NT-proBNP, and signs of heart failure (elevated JVP, third heart sound, crepitations). Management priorities are guideline-directed heart failure therapy with an ACE inhibitor and cautious beta-blocker introduction, strict exercise restriction for 3 to 6 months, and continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias. Cardiac MRI is the gold standard non-invasive investigation, demonstrating myocardial oedema on T2-weighted sequences and late gadolinium enhancement. NSAIDs are contraindicated in the presence of LV dysfunction.
key_points: Myocarditis is distinguished from pericarditis by significant troponin elevation, reduced LV function, and clinical heart failure
NSAIDs are contraindicated in myocarditis with LV dysfunction due to risk of worsening heart failure
Exercise restriction for 3 to 6 months is essential due to arrhythmia risk during the acute and recovery phases
explanation.pearls: Cardiac MRI confirms myocarditis using the updated Lake Louise criteria: T2-weighted sequences show myocardial oedema (acute inflammation) and late gadolinium enhancement shows myocardial necrosis or fibrosis. Exercise restriction should continue for 3 to 6 months with repeat imaging and normalisation of troponin and inflammatory markers before return to activity.

options.rationale: NSAIDs should be avoided in myocarditis with left ventricular dysfunction. While pericarditis and myocarditis may coexist, NSAIDs can worsen heart failure by promoting sodium and fluid retention and may increase myocardial damage in animal models of myocarditis. The predominant pathology here is myocarditis given the significant troponin elevation and reduced LVEF. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

This patient has acute myocarditis with significant left ventricular systolic dysfunction (EF 30%). Management includes guideline-directed heart failure therapy (ACE inhibitor or ARB and careful introduction of beta-blocker once stable), strict exercise restriction for 3 to 6 months, continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias, and cardiac MRI for diagnostic confirmation showing myocardial oedema and late gadolinium enhancement. NSAIDs are contraindicated with LV dysfunction. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

While the troponin is markedly elevated, the clinical context of a preceding viral illness in a young patient with global hypokinesis on echo (rather than regional wall motion abnormality) strongly suggests myocarditis. Coronary artery disease is unlikely in a 30-year-old without risk factors. Cardiac MRI is the preferred confirmatory investigation for myocarditis. Coronary angiography may be considered if the diagnosis remains uncertain. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Intravenous immunoglobulin has not been shown to improve outcomes in adult viral myocarditis and is not recommended as routine therapy. Management focuses on supportive care including heart failure therapy and monitoring for complications. Immunosuppression may be considered in specific subtypes such as giant cell myocarditis or eosinophilic myocarditis. (Source: UpToDate)

Empiric immunosuppression is not recommended for acute viral myocarditis and may worsen viral replication. Corticosteroids have a role in specific subtypes such as giant cell myocarditis, cardiac sarcoidosis, or eosinophilic myocarditis, but these require endomyocardial biopsy for confirmation before commencing immunosuppressive therapy. (Source: UpToDate)

explanation.summary: This patient presents with a hypertensive emergency defined by severely elevated blood pressure with acute target organ damage - in this case acute pulmonary oedema, acute kidney injury, and myocardial injury (elevated troponin). This is distinct from hypertensive urgency where blood pressure is severely elevated but without target organ damage. For hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema, glyceryl trinitrate infusion is the preferred agent as it reduces preload and pulmonary congestion through venodilation. Blood pressure should be reduced by no more than 25% of MAP in the first hour to prevent organ hypoperfusion, then gradually to 160/100 mmHg over the next 2 to 6 hours. Sodium nitroprusside carries cyanide toxicity risk, particularly with renal impairment.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency requires IV antihypertensive therapy; oral agents are inappropriate due to unpredictable onset and inability to titrate
GTN infusion is preferred for hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema due to its preload-reducing venodilatory effects
Target MAP reduction is no more than 25% in the first hour to avoid cerebral and coronary hypoperfusion
explanation.pearls: Glyceryl trinitrate infusion is commenced at 5 mcg/min and titrated every 5 minutes. Sodium nitroprusside should be avoided in renal impairment due to accumulation of the cyanide metabolite thiocyanate. In hypertensive emergency, the distinction between emergency (target organ damage present) and urgency (no target organ damage) determines whether IV or oral therapy is appropriate.

options.rationale: Sodium nitroprusside is a potent arterial and venous vasodilator but carries a risk of cyanide toxicity, particularly in patients with renal impairment as this patient has. It also requires invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring. Glyceryl trinitrate is preferred in hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema as it provides venodilation to reduce preload and has a more favourable safety profile. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Oral antihypertensive agents are not appropriate for hypertensive emergencies with acute target organ damage. They have unpredictable absorption and onset, making titration to blood pressure targets unreliable. This patient has acute pulmonary oedema, acute kidney injury, and hypoxaemic respiratory failure requiring intravenous therapy with careful blood pressure titration. ACE inhibitors are also relatively contraindicated acutely with hyperkalaemia and AKI. (Source: NHFA)

Labetalol is an appropriate intravenous agent for many hypertensive emergencies but is not the preferred choice when acute pulmonary oedema is the predominant target organ damage. Its negative inotropic effects from beta-blockade may worsen cardiac output in acute decompensated heart failure. Glyceryl trinitrate infusion is preferred as it reduces preload through venodilation and improves pulmonary congestion. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)

Intravenous enalaprilat is not widely available in Australia and is not first-line for hypertensive emergency with pulmonary oedema. In this patient, ACE inhibition is relatively contraindicated acutely due to the acute kidney injury (creatinine doubled from baseline) and hyperkalaemia (5.8 mmol/L), which may be worsened by renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade. (Source: AMH)

This patient has a hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema, AKI, and hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) infusion is the preferred first-line agent for hypertensive emergency complicated by acute pulmonary oedema. It acts primarily as a venodilator, reducing preload and pulmonary congestion, with arterial vasodilation at higher doses. The target is to reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour to avoid precipitating cerebral or coronary hypoperfusion. Concurrent management should include high-dose IV furosemide and consideration of non-invasive ventilation for respiratory support. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular)
